children.translated_text: Having bowed to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), the cause, and then to the sage <s>Kaṇāda</s>,
the <s>Padārthadharmasaṃgraha</s> (Compendium of Properties of Categories), which brings great benefit, shall be expounded.

body.translated_text: The knowledge of the true nature of the six <s>padārthas</s> (categories) — <s>dravya</s> (substance), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>sāmānya</s> (universal), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) — through their similarities and differences, is the cause of <s>niḥśreyasa</s> (supreme good).
And that arises only from <s>dharma</s> (merit), which is manifested by the command of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord).
Now, what are these <s>padārthas</s> (categories) beginning with <s>dravya</s> (substance)? And what are their similarities and differences?

Among these, the <s>dravyas</s> (substances), designated by the terms <s>sāmānya</s> (general) and <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), are nine only: <s>pṛthivī</s> (earth), <s>ap</s> (water), <s>tejas</s> (fire), <s>vāyu</s> (air), <s>ākāśa</s> (ether), <s>kāla</s> (time), <s>dik</s> (direction), <s>ātman</s> (self), and <s>manas</s> (mind) — because no other substance is designated by a name apart from these.

The <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) explicitly stated [by <s>Kaṇāda</s>] are seventeen: <s>rūpa</s> (color), <s>rasa</s> (taste), <s>gandha</s> (smell), <s>sparśa</s> (touch), <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number), <s>parimāṇa</s> (magnitude), <s>pṛthaktva</s> (distinctness), <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), <s>vibhāga</s> (disjunction), <s>paratva</s> (remoteness), <s>aparatva</s> (proximity), <s>buddhi</s> (cognition), <s>sukha</s> (pleasure), <s>duḥkha</s> (pain), <s>icchā</s> (desire), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>prayatna</s> (effort). And those gathered by the word 'ca' (and), not explicitly named, are seven only: <s>gurutva</s> (heaviness), <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity), <s>sneha</s> (viscosity), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency) — thus the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) are twenty-four in all.

The <s>karmas</s> (actions) are five only: throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and going. By the inclusion of 'going,' rotation, excretion, flowing, upward flaming, transverse blowing, bending, rising, and the like are specific kinds of going and not distinct types.

<s>Sāmānya</s> (universal) is of two kinds — <s>para</s> (highest) and <s>apara</s> (lower) — and is the cause of the cognition of commonality. Among these, the highest is <s>sattā</s> (existence), because it has the widest scope; and since it is the cause only of commonality, it is <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) alone. <s>Dravyatva</s> (substanceness) and the like are <s>apara</s> (lower), because they have a narrower scope; and since they are also the cause of differentiation, they receive the designation of <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) as well as <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity).
The ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities) reside in eternal substances. They are <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities) indeed, because they are the cause of absolute differentiation.

The relation that exists between entities that are inseparably connected and stand as container and contained, and that is the cause of the cognition 'this is in that' — that is <s>samavāya</s> (inherence).
Thus the enumeration of the category-bearers without their properties has been made.
All six <s>padārthas</s> (categories) possess existence, nameability, and knowability.
And dependence [on another] belongs to all except the eternal substances.
The five beginning with <s>dravya</s> (substance) possess the properties of being related by <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) and of being many.
The five beginning with <s>guṇa</s> (quality) possess the properties of being without qualities and without action.

The three beginning with <s>dravya</s> (substance) also possess connection with <s>sattā</s> (existence), the possession of <s>sāmānya</s> (universals) and <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularities), being denotable by words of their own system, and being the substratum of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit).
Being an effect and non-eternality belong only to those that have causes.
And causality belongs to all except <s>pārimāṇḍalya</s> (atomic sphericality) and the like.
And dependence on <s>dravya</s> (substance) belongs to all except the eternal substances.

The three beginning with <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) possess self-established existence, being characterized only by cognition, being non-effects, being non-causes, not having <s>sāmānya</s> (universals) and <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularities), eternality, and not being denotable by categorical words.

All nine beginning with <s>pṛthivī</s> (earth) possess connection with <s>dravyatva</s> (substanceness), being the originators of their own kind, possessing qualities, being incompatible with both effects and causes, and possessing ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities).
And non-dependence and eternality belong to all except the composite substances.
To <s>pṛthivī</s> (earth), <s>udaka</s> (water), <s>jvalana</s> (fire), <s>pavana</s> (air), <s>ātman</s> (self), and <s>manas</s> (mind) belong plurality and the possession of lower universals.

To <s>kṣiti</s> (earth), <s>jala</s> (water), <s>jyotis</s> (fire), <s>anila</s> (air), and <s>manas</s> (mind) belong the possession of action, corporeality, remoteness, proximity, and the possession of velocity.

To <s>ākāśa</s> (ether), <s>kāla</s> (time), <s>dik</s> (direction), and <s>ātman</s> (self) belong all-pervadingness, supreme magnitude, and having the same number of conjunctions as all conjoined entities.

To the five beginning with <s>pṛthivī</s> (earth) belong being elements, being the material cause of sense organs, being perceptible by one external sense organ, and possessing distinguishing qualities.
To the four belong being the originators of substances and possessing touch.
To the three belong perceptibility, possessing color, and fluidity.
To the two belong heaviness and possessing taste.
The elemental substances possess their own distinguishing qualities.
<s>Kṣiti</s> (earth) and <s>udaka</s> (water) and <s>ātman</s> (self) possess fourteen qualities.
<s>Ākāśa</s> (ether) and <s>ātman</s> (self) possess distinguishing qualities that reside momentarily in a single part.
<s>Dik</s> (direction) and <s>kāla</s> (time) possess five qualities and are the efficient cause of all produced things.
<s>Kṣiti</s> (earth) and <s>tejas</s> (fire) possess incidental fluidity.
Thus the similarities are to be stated in every case, and by their opposites the differences — in this way there is no confusion among the substances.
Now the differences shall be stated one by one.

<s>Pṛthivī</s> (earth) is that which is connected with <s>pṛthivītva</s> (earthness). It possesses <s>rūpa</s> (color), <s>rasa</s> (taste), <s>gandha</s> (smell), <s>sparśa</s> (touch), <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number), <s>parimāṇa</s> (magnitude), <s>pṛthaktva</s> (distinctness), <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), <s>vibhāga</s> (disjunction), <s>paratva</s> (remoteness), <s>aparatva</s> (proximity), <s>gurutva</s> (heaviness), <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency).

And these qualities — <s>rūpa</s> (color) and the rest — are established in the section on the assignment of qualities. From the statement 'perceptible by the eye,' the seven beginning with <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number) [are established]. From the teaching about falling, <s>gurutva</s> (heaviness) [is established]. From the statement 'common with water,' <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity) [is established]. From the statement 'subsequent action,' <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency) [is established].

<s>Gandha</s> (smell) belongs to <s>kṣiti</s> (earth) alone. <s>Rūpa</s> (color) is of many kinds — white and so forth. <s>Rasa</s> (taste) is of six kinds — sweet and so forth. <s>Gandha</s> (smell) is of two kinds — fragrant and non-fragrant. Its <s>sparśa</s> (touch), being neither hot nor cold, is produced by <s>pāka</s> (heating).

It is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That characterized as <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom) is eternal. That characterized as an effect is non-eternal. And it, distinguished by specific arrangements of parts such as solidity and so on, endowed with plurality and lower universals, serves many purposes such as beds, seats, and the like. And its effects are threefold, designated as body, sense organ, and object.

The body is of two kinds: born from a womb and not born from a womb. Among these, the non-womb-born, without depending on semen and blood, arises from atoms accompanied by special <s>dharma</s> (merit) — [this is the body] of gods and sages.

The bodies of small creatures and those in places of torment arise from atoms accompanied by special <s>adharma</s> (demerit). That born from the union of semen and blood is womb-born. It is of various kinds: viviparous and oviparous. For humans, cattle, and wild animals it is viviparous. For birds and reptiles it is oviparous.

The sense organ [of earth] is the organ of smell: it manifests <s>gandha</s> (smell) and is produced in all living beings from earthy parts not overwhelmed by water and other elements — this is <s>ghrāṇa</s> (the nose).

The object is threefold, produced through the sequence of dyads and so forth, and is characterized as clay, stone, and plants. Among these, the clay varieties are tracts of land, walls, bricks, and the like. Stones are rocks, gems, diamonds, and the like. Plants are grasses, herbs, trees, shrubs, creepers, spreading vines, and forest trees.

<s>Āpas</s> (water) is that which is connected with <s>aptva</s> (waterness). It possesses <s>rūpa</s> (color), <s>rasa</s> (taste), <s>sparśa</s> (touch), <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity), <s>sneha</s> (viscosity), <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number), <s>parimāṇa</s> (magnitude), <s>pṛthaktva</s> (distinctness), <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), <s>vibhāga</s> (disjunction), <s>paratva</s> (remoteness), <s>aparatva</s> (proximity), <s>gurutva</s> (heaviness), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency).
The establishment of these is as before.

Its <s>rūpa</s> (color), <s>rasa</s> (taste), and <s>sparśa</s> (touch) are exclusively white, sweet, and cold respectively. <s>Sneha</s> (viscosity) belongs to water alone, and <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity) is natural to it.
And these are of two kinds, as before, due to the distinction of eternal and non-eternal. Their effects are threefold, designated as body, sense organ, and object.
Among these, the body is non-womb-born only, in the world of <s>Varuṇa</s>, and is capable of enjoyment due to the support of earthy parts.
The sense organ is the organ of taste: it manifests <s>rasa</s> (taste) in all living beings and is produced from watery parts not overwhelmed by other elements — this is <s>rasana</s> (the tongue).
The objects are rivers, oceans, hail, dew, and the like.

<s>Tejas</s> (fire) is that which is connected with <s>tejastva</s> (fireness). It possesses <s>rūpa</s> (color), <s>sparśa</s> (touch), <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number), <s>parimāṇa</s> (magnitude), <s>pṛthaktva</s> (distinctness), <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), <s>vibhāga</s> (disjunction), <s>paratva</s> (remoteness), <s>aparatva</s> (proximity), <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency).
The establishment of these is as before.
Its <s>rūpa</s> (color) is white and luminous. Its <s>sparśa</s> (touch) is exclusively hot.
It too is of two kinds, due to the distinction of atom and effect. And its effects are the triad of body and so forth.
The body is non-womb-born, in the world of <s>Āditya</s> (the Sun), and is capable of enjoyment due to the support of earthy parts.

The sense organ is the organ of sight: it manifests <s>rūpa</s> (color) in all living beings and is produced from fiery parts not overwhelmed by other elemental parts — this is <s>cakṣus</s> (the eye).

That designated as object is fourfold: terrestrial, celestial, abdominal, and mineral. Among these, the terrestrial is that produced from wood and fuel, whose nature is upward flaming, and which is capable of cooking, burning, causing perspiration, and so on. The celestial is without fuel — solar, lightning, and the like. The abdominal is for the transformation of consumed food into <s>rasa</s> (essence) and so forth. And the mineral is gold and the like.
In these, the perception of <s>rasa</s> (taste) and the like is through the relation of being in contact with what is in <s>samavāya</s> (inherence).

<s>Vāyu</s> (air) is that which is connected with <s>vāyutva</s> (airness). It possesses <s>sparśa</s> (touch), <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number), <s>parimāṇa</s> (magnitude), <s>pṛthaktva</s> (distinctness), <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), <s>vibhāga</s> (disjunction), <s>paratva</s> (remoteness), <s>aparatva</s> (proximity), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency).

Its <s>sparśa</s> (touch), being neither hot nor cold, is not produced by <s>pāka</s> (heating). It is established from the assignment of qualities. From the statement 'among the formless, not perceptible by the eye,' the seven beginning with <s>saṃkhyā</s> (number) [are established]. From the statement about the action of grass, <s>saṃskāra</s> (tendency) [is established].
And this too is of two kinds, due to the distinction of atom and effect.
Among these, the effect-form is fourfold: body, sense organ, object, and <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath).
Among these, the non-womb-born body alone of the wind-gods (<s>Marut</s>) in the world is capable of enjoyment due to the support of earth-atoms.
The sense organ of all living beings that apprehends touch, composed of wind-atoms not overpowered by earth and the others, pervading the entire body — that is the skin-organ (<s>tvagindriya</s>).

Its object, being the substratum of apprehended touch, characterized by touch, sound, momentum, and vibration, of the nature of lateral movement, and capable of impelling and sustaining clouds and so forth.

Although imperceptible, its multiplicity is inferred from collision. Collision, moreover, is the meeting of two winds of equal velocity moving in opposite directions. This too is inferred from the upward movement of two composite winds; and that again from the movement of grass and so forth.

<s>Prāṇa</s> (the vital breath), being a single cause of the propulsion of fluids, waste, and bodily constituents within the body, receives the designations <s>apāna</s> and so forth due to differences in activity.
Now here the method of creation and dissolution of the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>) is described.

At the end of a hundred years of <s>Brahmā</s>, at the time of final liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) of the present <s>Brahmā</s>, when all living beings wearied of <s>saṃsāra</s> need rest at night, simultaneously with the desire of <s>Maheśvara</s>, the lord of all worlds, to withdraw — when the cessation of activity of the unseen merits (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) residing in all souls, which bind body, sense organs, and great elements, occurs — from the actions born of the conjunction of <s>Maheśvara</s>'s will and the atoms of the souls, the constituent atoms that are the causes of body and sense organs separate from their conjunctions, and there is destruction of them down to the ultimate atoms.

Likewise, of earth, water, fire, and wind — the great elements too — in this very order, when each succeeding one exists, the preceding one is destroyed. Thereupon, the atoms remain separately, and the souls, pervaded by the impressions of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, remain for that same duration of time.

Then again, for the enjoyment of living beings, immediately after <s>Maheśvara</s>'s desire to create, from the conjunctions dependent on the unseen merit whose activity has been obtained in all souls, when action arises in the wind-atoms, from their mutual conjunctions in the order of dyads and so forth, a great wind comes into being and remains, tossing about in space.

Immediately thereafter, in that very wind, from those water-atoms, in that very order, a great ocean comes into being and remains, floating. Immediately thereafter, in that very water, from earth-atoms, in the order of dyads and so forth, the great earth comes into being and remains consolidated.
Immediately thereafter, in that very great ocean, from fire-atoms, in the order of dyads and so forth, a great mass of fire comes into being and remains, blazing, being overpowered by nothing.

When the four great elements have thus arisen, merely through the contemplation of <s>Maheśvara</s>, from fire-atoms combined with earth-atoms, a great cosmic egg (<s>aṇḍa</s>) is produced. In that, having produced four-faced <s>Brahmā</s>, the grandfather of all worlds, together with the entire universe, he appoints him to the creation of beings.

And he, <s>Brahmā</s>, appointed by <s>Maheśvara</s>, endowed with supreme knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, having understood the ripening of the <s>karma</s> of living beings, creates through mind the sons — <s>Prajāpatis</s>, divine sages, ancestral hosts — and from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the four <s>varṇas</s>, and other high and low beings, and endows them with <s>dharma</s>, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty according to their dispositions.

Space (<s>ākāśa</s>), time (<s>kāla</s>), and direction (<s>dik</s>) — since each is singular, in the absence of congeners, three conventional designations are given: 'space,' 'time,' and 'direction.' Of these, the qualities of space are: sound, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.

Sound, though perceptible, because it is not preceded by a causal quality, because it does not persist as long as the substance, because it is apprehended elsewhere than in its substrate — is not a specific quality like touch. Because it is perceptible to the external sense organ, because it is grasped by another internal organ, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is grasped distinctly from the ego-sense — it is not a quality of the self.

Because it is grasped by the ear, and because of its character as a particular quality — it does not belong to direction, time, or mind. By the method of residues, being a quality, it is the inferential mark for the cognition of space. Because the inferential mark of sound is not different, the unity of space is established.

From the conformity with that, separateness is established. From the statement that it is all-pervading, it has the supremely great dimension. From the statement that it is the cause of sound, conjunction and disjunction are established.

Therefore, from possessing qualities and from not being dependent on another, it is a substance. From the absence of a homogeneous or heterogeneous cause, it is eternal. And it is the condition for the apprehension of sound by all living beings, through the nature of the ear.

The ear, moreover, is the region of space designated as the cavity of hearing, connected with <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> that bring about the enjoyment of the object conditioned by sound. And when space is eternal, deafness arises from the deficiency of the connecting factors.

Time (<s>kāla</s>) is indicated by the marks of priority and posteriority, their interchange, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, and quickness and slowness. When cognitions distinct from prior cognitions arise in their objects and no other cause is found — that which is the cause here is time.

And it is the cause of the origination, persistence, and destruction of all effects, as declared. It is the cause of the conventional usage of moment, instant, wink, <s>kāṣṭhā</s>, <s>kalā</s>, <s>muhūrta</s>, <s>yāma</s>, day-and-night, fortnight, month, season, half-year, year, <s>yuga</s>, <s>kalpa</s>, <s>manvantara</s>, dissolution, and great dissolution.

Its qualities are: number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. Because the inferential mark of time is not different, its unity is established. From conformity with that, separateness. From the statement 'time is the cause,' the supremely great dimension. From the statement of causality, priority, and so forth, conjunction.

Because it destroys that, disjunction. Its substancehood and eternality are established like those of space. Although strictly singular because the inferential mark of time is not different, the figurative attribution of multiplicity is made — like a jewel or a cooking agent — due to the distinctions of origination, activity, completion, persistence, cessation, and conditions of production of all effects.

Direction (<s>dik</s>) is indicated by the cognitions of east, west, and so forth. Taking a corporeal substance as a reference point, the ten cognitions that arise among corporeal substances — 'this is east of that,' 'south,' 'west,' 'north,' 'southeast,' 'southwest,' 'northwest,' 'northeast,' 'below,' and 'above' — that from which they arise is direction.
Because no other cause is possible.

Its qualities are: number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction — these are established as for time. Although direction is strictly singular because its inferential mark is not different, the directions have been given ten designations such as 'eastern' and so forth by the supreme sages, for the purpose of conventional usage in <s>Śruti</s>, <s>Smṛti</s>, and the world, based on the particular conjunctions of the world-regions presided over by the world-guardians, as the blessed sun revolves clockwise around <s>Meru</s>. Hence, by convention, the ten directions are established.

From the very fact that those are presided over by deities, there are again ten designations: <s>Māhendrī</s> (of Indra), <s>Vaiśvānarī</s> (of Agni), <s>Yāmyā</s> (of Yama), <s>Nairṛtī</s> (of Nirṛti), <s>Vāruṇī</s> (of Varuṇa), <s>Vāyavyā</s> (of Vāyu), <s>Kauverī</s> (of Kubera), <s>Aiśānī</s> (of Īśāna), <s>Brāhmī</s> (of Brahmā), and <s>Nāgī</s> (of the Nāgas).

Due to its connection with selfhood, [it is called] <s>ātman</s> (self). Though it is imperceptible on account of its subtlety, knowledge of it is obtained through the instruments [of cognition] — namely, the ear and other sense organs, which are inferred from the apprehension of sound and other [sense objects]. Since instruments such as the adze and the like are seen to be employed by an agent, and since there is established [apprehension] regarding sounds and the like, an agent is inferred [behind them].

It is not [an attribute] of the body, sense organs, or mind, because they are non-cognizing. Consciousness does not belong to the body, because it is an effect of the elements, like a pot, and because it does not occur in a dead body. Nor does it belong to the sense organs, because they are [mere] instruments, and because recollection is observed even when the sense organs are impaired and the objects are not present.

Nor does it belong to the mind, because if [the mind] did not depend on another instrument, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous perception and recollection, and because [the mind] itself has the nature of an instrument. By the method of elimination, since [cognition] is the effect of the <s>ātman</s>, the <s>ātman</s> is thereby established. And from the activities and cessations [of the body] that are conjoined with the body — which are capable of the attainment and avoidance of the beneficial and the harmful — an agent possessing effort is inferred as the controller of the body, like a charioteer through the action of the chariot. And also through vital breath and the like.

How so? From the observation of the modified action of the wind that has been taken up by the body — like one who operates bellows — from the regular action of opening and closing the eyelids — like the operator of a wooden puppet — from being the cause of the growth, healing of wounds, and mending of fractures of the body —

like a householder, through the connection of instruments that grasp desired objects by means of the activity of the mind — like one who moves puppets in the corners of a house; like a boy, after seeing with the eye-faculty, from the observation of the activity of the tongue in the sequence of recollecting taste — like a spectator inside [a house] with many windows — a single [entity] is known as the seer of both [internal and external objects].

And from the qualities of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, a possessor of qualities is inferred. And those are not qualities of the body or sense organs. Why? Because there is no co-referential unity with the ego-notion (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>); because they exist in specific locations; because they do not last as long as the substance; and because they are not perceptible to the external sense organs. Likewise, through the word 'I' (<s>aham</s>), because it is distinct from words like 'earth' and 'celestial' and so forth.

Its qualities are: cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), effort (<s>prayatna</s>), merit (<s>dharma</s>), demerit (<s>adharma</s>), dispositional tendency (<s>saṃskāra</s>), number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), dimension (<s>parimāṇa</s>), distinctness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), conjunction (<s>samyoga</s>), and disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>). In the section on the marks of the <s>ātman</s>, [the qualities] from cognition up to effort are established.

<s>Dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) [are established] from the statement that they are not the cause of other qualities inherent in the <s>ātman</s>. <s>Saṃskāra</s> (dispositional tendency) [is established] from the statement that it is a cause in the production of memory. Number and distinctness too, for the same reason, from the statement of systematic arrangement. And from the statement 'ātman,' the supremely great dimension is [established].
Conjunction [is established] because pleasures and the like arise from contact. Disjunction, because it is the destroyer of that [conjunction].

The mind [is established] from the statement '<s>manas</s>' (mind) through [its] connection. Even when the <s>ātman</s>, sense organs, and objects are present, since cognition, pleasure, and the like are observed to arise having previously not existed, another instrument [besides the external senses] is inferred. From the observation that memory arises even when the ear and other [external senses] are not functioning, and because there is an internal faculty that apprehends pleasure and the like, which are not grasped by the external sense organs — therefore [it is] an internal instrument.

Its qualities are: number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), dimension (<s>parimāṇa</s>), distinctness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), conjunction (<s>samyoga</s>), disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>), remoteness (<s>paratva</s>), proximity (<s>aparatva</s>), and dispositional tendency (<s>saṃskāra</s>). From the statement of the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition, its oneness per body is established. Its distinctness too, for the same reason. From the statement of the absence of that [dimension], its atomic dimension is established.

From the statement of departure and approach, conjunction and disjunction [are established]. Because it is corporeal (<s>mūrta</s>), remoteness and proximity [are established], and also dispositional tendency. Because it lacks the quality of tangibility, it does not produce substances. Because it possesses action, it is corporeal. Because of the undesirable consequence of having a commonly shared body, it is non-cognizing.

Because it has the nature of an instrument, it exists for the sake of another. Because it possesses qualities, it is a substance. And because it is under the control of effort and unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), it moves swiftly.
Thus [ends] the category of substance (<s>dravyapadārtha</s>) in the commentary of <s>Praśastapāda</s>.
Now the examination of the category of quality (<s>guṇapadārtha</s>).

The connection with quality-hood (<s>guṇatva</s>) [that is common] to all qualities such as color (<s>rūpa</s>) and the rest [means]: dependence on substances, absence of [further] qualities, and absence of activity.

Color (<s>rūpa</s>), taste (<s>rasa</s>), smell (<s>gandha</s>), touch (<s>sparśa</s>), remoteness (<s>paratva</s>), proximity (<s>aparatva</s>), heaviness (<s>gurutva</s>), fluidity (<s>dravatva</s>), viscosity (<s>sneha</s>), and impetus (<s>vega</s>) are qualities of corporeal [substances].

Cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), effort (<s>prayatna</s>), merit (<s>dharma</s>), demerit (<s>adharma</s>), impression (<s>bhāvanā</s>), and sound (<s>śabda</s>) are qualities of incorporeal [substances].

Number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), dimension (<s>parimāṇa</s>), distinctness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), conjunction (<s>samyoga</s>), and disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>) are qualities of both [corporeal and incorporeal substances].
Conjunction, disjunction, duality (<s>dvitva</s>), binary distinctness (<s>dvipṛthaktva</s>), and so forth reside in multiple substrata.
The remaining [qualities] reside in one substance each.
Color, taste, smell, touch, viscosity, natural fluidity, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, impression, and sound are specific qualities (<s>vaiśeṣikaguṇa</s>).
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, heaviness, occasioned fluidity, and impetus are common qualities (<s>sāmānyaguṇa</s>).
Sound, touch, color, taste, and smell are each grasped by a single external sense organ.
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, fluidity, viscosity, and impetus are grasped by two sense organs.
Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are grasped by the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>).
Heaviness, merit, demerit, and impression are indeed beyond the senses (<s>atīndriya</s>).
Non-heat-produced color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, oneness, singular distinctness, heaviness, fluidity, viscosity, and impetus are preceded by qualities of the cause.
Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, impression, and sound are not preceded by qualities of the cause.

Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, impression, sound, cotton-dimension, subsequent conjunction, occasioned fluidity, remoteness, proximity, and heat-produced [qualities] are produced by conjunction.
Conjunction, disjunction, and impetus are produced by action (<s>karma</s>).
Sound and subsequent disjunction are produced by disjunction.
Remoteness, proximity, duality, binary distinctness, and so forth are dependent on cognition (<s>buddhyapekṣa</s>).
Color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, sound, dimension, oneness, singular distinctness, and viscosity produce [effects] of the same kind.
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort do not produce [effects] of the same kind.
Conjunction, disjunction, number, heaviness, fluidity, hot touch, cognition, merit, demerit, and dispositional tendency produce [effects] of both the same and different kinds.
Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, impression, and sound produce [effects] in what is co-inherent with their own substratum.
Color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, viscosity, and effort produce [effects] elsewhere.
Conjunction, disjunction, number, singular distinctness, heaviness, fluidity, impetus, merit, and demerit produce [effects] in both [their own substratum and elsewhere].
Heaviness, fluidity, impetus, effort, merit, demerit, and specific conjunctions are causes of activity.
Color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, number, dimension, singular distinctness, viscosity, and sound have the nature of non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>).
Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and impression have the nature of efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>).
Conjunction, disjunction, hot touch, heaviness, fluidity, and impetus have causality in both ways.
Remoteness, proximity, duality, binary distinctness, and so forth are non-causes.
Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities of the <s>ātman</s> exist in specific locations.
The remaining [qualities] pervade [the entire extent of] their substratum.
Non-heat-produced color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, oneness, singular distinctness, natural fluidity, heaviness, and viscosity last as long as the substance lasts.
The remaining [qualities] do not last as long as the substance.
All qualities such as color and the rest receive their designations as 'color' and so forth from their respective connection with the particular universal (<s>aparasāmānya</s>).

Among these, color (<s>rūpa</s>) is grasped by the eye. It resides in earth, water, and fire. It is the cause of apprehending substances and the like, a cooperating factor of vision, of many kinds such as white and so forth. In the atoms of water and the like, it is eternal; in the atoms of earth, it is opposed by contact with fire. In all produced substances, it is preceded by qualities of the cause. It perishes only through the destruction of its substratum.

Taste (<s>rasa</s>) is grasped by the tongue. It resides in earth and water. It is the cause of sustenance, nourishment, strength, and health; a cooperating factor of the tongue; divided into the varieties of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. Its eternal and non-eternal production is like that of color.

Smell (<s>gandha</s>) is grasped by the nose. It resides in earth. It is a cooperating factor of the nose. It is either pleasant (<s>surabhi</s>) or unpleasant (<s>asurabhi</s>). Its origination and other [characteristics] are explained as before.

<s>Sparśa</s> (touch) is apprehended by the organ of touch (skin). It is the activity of earth, water, fire, and wind. It cooperates with the skin. It follows after <s>rūpa</s> (form). It is of three kinds, according to the division into cold, hot, and neither cold nor hot. Its determinations as eternal and non-eternal are also as stated before.

The method of production through transformation by fire (<s>pākaja</s>) of the <s>rūpa</s> (form) and other qualities of earthly atoms is as follows: When a raw substance such as a pot, connected with fire, is struck by fire or subjected to impact, <s>karmas</s> (motions) arise in the atoms that compose it. From these arise separations (<s>vibhāga</s>); from the separations arise destructions of conjunctions; and from the destructions of conjunctions, the effect-substance is destroyed.

When that is destroyed, in the independent atoms, through conjunction with fire and in dependence on heat, destruction of the dark colors and so forth occurs. Then again, from another conjunction with fire and in dependence on heat, transformation-born (<s>pākaja</s>) qualities arise.

Immediately thereafter, through the conjunction of the self with the atoms, dependent on the unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) of the enjoyers, when motions arise in the atoms that have acquired transformation-born qualities, from their mutual conjunction, the effect-substance is produced in the sequence of dyads and so forth. And therein, the production of <s>rūpa</s> (form) and other qualities follows the pattern of the cause-qualities.

But the production or destruction of <s>rūpa</s> and other qualities cannot occur in the effect-substance itself, because fire, being present both inside and outside in all the parts, cannot pervade it; and even through the entry of atoms, pervation is not possible, because that would require the destruction of the effect-substance.

<s>Saṃkhyā</s> (number) is the cause of the conventional usage of 'one' and so forth. It is of two kinds: residing in one substance and residing in many substances. Of these, the number residing in one substance—like the <s>rūpa</s> and other qualities of water-atoms and the like—has its determinations as eternal and non-eternal as stated before. The number residing in many substances is duality and so forth, up to the highest number (<s>parārdha</s>).

Its production is from the unitinesses (<s>ekatvas</s>) accompanied by a cognition having multiple objects; and its destruction is from the destruction of the relational cognition (<s>apekṣābuddhi</s>). How so?

When, for a cognizer, there is contact through the eye with two substances—whether of the same or different class—and when there arises the cognition of the universal 'unitiness' (<s>ekatvasāmānya</s>) conjoined with and inherent in them, then from the cognitions of the relation with the universal 'unitiness,' a single cognition having multiple objects arises with respect to the two possessors of the quality of unitiness. Then, dependent on that cognition, duality (<s>dvitva</s>) is produced in its two substrates from the two unitinesses. Then again, the cognition of the universal 'duality' (<s>dvitvasāmānya</s>) arises in that. From that cognition of the universal 'duality,' while the relational cognition is being destroyed, and while the cognition of the quality of duality is being produced from the universal 'duality,' its relation, and their cognitions—this constitutes one moment.

Now then, while the quality of duality is being destroyed due to the destruction of the relational cognition, and while the cognition of the quality of duality—which is the cause of the destruction of the cognition of the universal 'duality'—together with the cognition of the substance 'these are two substances' is being produced from the quality of duality, its cognition, and their relation—this constitutes one moment.

Immediately thereafter, the production of the substance-cognition 'these are two substances' occurs, the destruction of duality occurs, and while the cognition of the quality of duality is being destroyed, a <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) is being produced from the substance-cognition—this constitutes one moment. Immediately thereafter, from the substance-cognition comes the destruction of the cognition of the quality of duality, and of the substance-cognition itself from the <s>saṃskāra</s>.

By this, the production of triplicity and so forth is also explained: production is from unitinesses accompanied by a cognition having multiple objects, and destruction is from the destruction of the relational cognition. And in some cases, from the destruction of the substrate. How so?

When a motion arises in a part that is the substrate of unitiness, at that very time the cognition of the universal 'unitiness' arises. And by the motion, a separation from another part is effected. And the production of the relational cognition occurs.

Then, at the very moment when the destruction of conjunction occurs due to the separation, at that very moment duality is produced. From the destruction of conjunction comes the destruction of the substance. And the production of the universal-cognition also occurs.

Then, at the very moment when the destruction of the relational cognition occurs due to the cognition of the universal, at that very moment, from the destruction of the substrate, the destruction of duality occurs. This procedure is elegant in the theory of mutual destruction (<s>badhyaghātaka</s>); but in the theory of conflict characterized by non-coexistence (<s>sahānavasthānalakṣaṇa</s>), there would be the consequence of the non-production of substance-cognition. How so?

If duality is destroyed simultaneously with the quality-cognition due to the destruction of the relational cognition, then the substance-cognition 'these are two substances,' which depends on that duality, would not arise—that is the problematic consequence. If someone thinks that, just like inferential knowledge, from mere cognition alone [it could arise]—that is, just as in the case of 'what existed, existed,' where there is inference from mere cognition even in the absence of the logical mark—so too, even when the quality is destroyed, from the mere cognition of the quality, the cognition of the substance could arise—

No. Because it is a qualified cognition. For a qualified cognition cannot arise from mere similarity alone without the connection of the qualifier. And thus the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras) says: 'From the whiteness inherent in a substance, the cognition of whiteness, and from that the cognition of the white—these are in a cause-effect relationship.'

Inferential cognition, however, does not arise through non-difference. Therefore this comparison is inappropriate. There is no fault of rapidity of arising—just as in 'sound is like space,' where three cognitions arise rapidly, so too in the arising of the cognition of duality and so forth, there is no defect.

If one thinks there is the same defect in the mutual destruction theory as well—one might think: surely in the mutual destruction theory too, there would be the consequence of non-production of substance-cognition. How? Because of the destruction of the relational cognition from the <s>saṃskāra</s> simultaneously with the cognition of the universal 'duality.' No.

Because the aggregate-cognition is the cause of the <s>saṃskāra</s>. It is the aggregate-cognition alone that causes the <s>saṃskāra</s>, not the perceptual cognition. Thus there is no defect. If one thinks there would be the consequence of simultaneous cognitions—one might think: in the mutual destruction theory of cognitions, there would be the consequence of simultaneous cognitions. No.
Because co-existence of two non-perishing things is prohibited.

By the statement prohibiting simultaneous cognitions, what is prohibited is the simultaneous arising of two cognitions and the simultaneous abiding of two non-perishing cognitions. For in the mutual destruction theory, there is neither simultaneous arising of cognitions nor simultaneous abiding of perishing cognitions.

<s>Parimāṇa</s> (dimension/magnitude) is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement. It is of four kinds: <s>aṇu</s> (atomic/minute), <s>mahat</s> (great/large), <s>dīrgha</s> (long), and <s>hrasva</s> (short). Of these, the great is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is the supreme greatness in space, time, direction, and the self. The non-eternal is found in triads and so forth.

Likewise, the minute is also of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is the globularity (<s>pārimāṇḍalya</s>) in atoms and minds. The non-eternal is found only in dyads. In things that are large, such as a lotus fruit, <s>āmalaka</s> fruit, <s>bilva</s> fruit, and so forth, the conventional usage of 'minuteness' is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of a higher degree of that quality.

Longness and shortness are also produced, and are co-inherent with greatness and minuteness respectively. In things that are directly long, such as a stick, sugarcane, bamboo, and so forth, the conventional usage of 'shortness' is figurative, depending on the presence or absence of a higher degree of that quality.

The non-eternal fourfold dimension is born from number, dimension, and accumulation (<s>pracaya</s>). Of these, the number 'multiplicity' (<s>bahutva</s>), produced in dependence on the cognition of the Lord in atoms and dyads, produces greatness and longness simultaneously with the production of <s>rūpa</s> (form) and other qualities in the effect-substance—the triad and so forth—composed from them.

In an effect-substance composed of two or more great components, it is the greatnesses of the causes alone that produce greatness, not multiplicity—because we observe excess even in substances composed of the same number of components.

Accumulation (<s>pracaya</s>), present in two cotton bundles and depending on the loose conjunctions of the parts composing one bundle or depending on the conjunctions of the parts of each bundle with each other, produces greatness in the double cotton bundle, not multiplicity or greatness.

Because we observe excess even in substances composed of components of the same number and the same weight-dimension. And the number of duality, present in the atoms, produces minuteness in the dyad. As with greatness, in triads and so forth, the production of longness comes from accumulations of the same class as the multiplicity-greatness of the causes.

As with minuteness, in the dyad, the production of shortness comes from the number of duality. Now, what is the distinction between greatness and longness, which exist in triads and so forth, from each other? And between minuteness and shortness in dyads?

In that regard, there is indeed a distinction between greatness and longness from each other, because we observe distinct conventional usage: 'let the long be brought among the large ones, and let the large be brought among the long ones.'

But the distinction between minuteness and shortness from each other is direct perception for those who perceive them. And all four kinds of dimension, being produced, are destroyed only from the destruction of the substrate.

<s>Pṛthaktva</s> (separateness) is the cause of the usage based on mental abstraction. It is further of two kinds: residing in one substance and residing in many substances. Its determinations as eternal and non-eternal have been explained under number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>). The distinguishing point is this: in the case of one-separateness and so forth, there is no higher universal, unlike oneness and so forth; but it is distinguished by number, because we observe usage distinguished by it.

<s>Saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) is the instrumental cause of the cognition 'conjoined.' It is also the cause of substances, qualities, and actions. In the origination of substance, it is independent (<s>nirapekṣa</s>), as stated: 'it is thus, from both dependent and independent causes.' But in the origination of qualities and actions, it is dependent, as stated: 'the specific quality of fire comes from conjunction-inherence.'

Now, what is its definition, and how many kinds are there? The coming together of things previously apart — that is <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction). It is of three kinds: produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by conjunction.

An example of conjunction produced by the action of one is when something moving meets something stationary, as a hawk meets a post, or as all-pervading substances meet embodied ones. Conjunction produced by the action of both is the meeting of two things moving in opposite directions, as with two wrestlers or two rams.

Conjunction produced by conjunction, however, is the conjunction between a newly arisen or long-existing stationary thing and things conjoined with its cause but which are not themselves causes — a conjunction preceded by the conjunction of cause and non-cause, residing in effect and non-effect.

Such conjunction arises from one, from two, and from many causes. From one: from the conjunction of a thread with a reed, the conjunction of a two-threaded thing with the reed. From two: from two conjunctions of thread and space, a single conjunction of a two-threaded thing with space. From many: from the conjunctions of threads and a loom, a single conjunction of cloth and loom.

And from a single conjunction, the origination of two: How? When, there being conjunction between an earthy atom and a watery atom, another earthy atom simultaneously conjoins with the earthy one and another watery atom with the watery one, then by those two conjunctions, an earthy and a watery <s>dvyaṇuka</s> (dyad) are simultaneously produced.

Then, at the time when qualities such as color arise in the dyads through the sequence of causal qualities, at that very time, from the conjunction residing in each one's cause-and-non-cause, conjunctions residing in each one's effect-and-non-effect are simultaneously produced. What is the reason?

For the principle is: the effect necessarily conjoins with a non-cause that is conjoined with the cause. Therefore, the earthy <s>dvyaṇuka</s> (dyad) is connected with the watery atom conjoined with the cause, and the watery <s>dvyaṇuka</s> is connected with the earthy atom conjoined with the cause.

Now, when the two dyads are connected through each other's cause-and-non-cause, how is there a mutual connection between them? For them too, the connection is through conjunctions produced by conjunction. There is no beginningless conjunction, as with the eternally spherical (<s>parimaṇḍala</s>), since it is not separately mentioned.

Just as, having stated the four kinds of measure as produced, he says 'the spherical is eternal' — so having stated conjunction produced by the action of one and so forth as produced, he would separately say 'eternal,' but he did not say so. Therefore, there is no beginningless conjunction.

The conjunction of atoms with space and the like, residing in a limited region, is conjunction produced by the action of one. But between all-pervading substances there is no mutual conjunction, due to the absence of <s>yutasiddhi</s> (separate existence).

<s>Yutasiddhi</s> (separate existence), in turn, is the possession of independent motion by both or either of the two, and the relationship of support and supported in separate substrata. Destruction of all conjunction occurs through disjunction inherent in the same locus, and sometimes also through destruction of the substratum. How?

When, there being conjunction of two threads, an action arises in a portion (<s>aṃśa</s>) that originates one of the threads, that action produces disjunction from the other portion; from disjunction comes the destruction of the conjunction originating the thread; from the destruction of conjunction comes the destruction of the thread; and upon its destruction, the destruction of the conjunction with the other thread that was supported by it.

<s>Vibhāga</s> (disjunction) is the instrumental cause of the cognition 'disjoined.' It is also the cause of the disjunction of sound. Disjunction is the separation preceded by prior contact. It is of three kinds: produced by the action of one, produced by the action of both, and produced by disjunction.

Of these, disjunction produced by the action of one and produced by the action of both are like conjunction. But disjunction produced by disjunction is of two kinds: from causal disjunction and from cause-non-cause disjunction. Of these, from causal disjunction: when an action arises in a cause pervaded by an effect, it produces disjunction from the other part, not at that time from the spatial region of space and the like; but when it produces disjunction from the spatial region of space and the like, not at that time from the other part — such is the established position.

Therefore, the action of the part produces disjunction from the other part only; from that disjunction comes the destruction of the conjunction originating the substance; upon its destruction, from the absence of cause comes the absence of effect — thus the destruction of the composite thing. Then the disjunction existing between the causes, awaiting a subsequent moment distinguished by the destruction of the effect or an independent part, of the moving part only that is conjoined with the effect, produces disjunction from the spatial region of space and the like — not of the stationary part, due to absence of cause. There would be the undesirable consequence of non-utilization in the case of non-production of subsequent conjunction. But the action of that part does not produce disjunction from the spatial region of space and the like, since the time of its production has passed; however, it does produce conjunction with another spatial region, since there is no lapse of time for the action that has not yet produced conjunction.
How from cause-non-cause disjunction also?

When an action arises in the hand and, not producing disjunction from the other part, produces disjunctions from spatial regions of space and the like and conjunctions with other regions, then those cause-non-cause disjunctions, with respect to the direction toward which the action is oriented for producing the effect, produce disjunctions between effect and non-effect; and immediately after that, conjunctions between effect and non-effect from the conjunction of cause and non-cause.

If, immediately after causal disjunction, the disjunction of the effect arises, and immediately after causal conjunction, the conjunction of the effect arises — then would there not be the undesirable consequence of <s>yutasiddhi</s> (separate existence) of part and whole? No.

Due to non-comprehension of <s>yutasiddhi</s> (separate existence). <s>Yutasiddhi</s>, again, is the possession of independent motion by both or either of the two; but for non-eternal entities, inherence in separate substrata constitutes <s>yutasiddhi</s>.

Between the skin-organ and the body, there is no independent motion, but there is inherence in separate substrata — hence their mutual conjunction is established. Between an atom and space, however, even in the absence of a different substratum, conjunction and disjunction are established because one of them possesses independent motion.

Between thread and cloth, both being non-eternal, there is absence of mutual conjunction and disjunction due to absence of a different substratum. Between space and the like, due to absence of independent motion, there is absence of mutual conjunction and disjunction.
The destruction of all disjunction is momentary, due to its momentary nature, from the existence of a subsequent conjunction as its limit.

But disjunction does not exist only between conjoined things; nor does destruction of those two occur only from their conjunction. Why? Because the continued occurrence of the cognition 'disjoined' does not persist like that of 'conjoined.' Therefore, due to the existence of a subsequent conjunction as limit, it is momentary.
And sometimes it perishes simply from the destruction of the substratum. How?

When an action arises in a portion that is a cause of a <s>dvyaṇuka</s> (dyad) and produces disjunction from the other portion, at that very time an action also arises in the other thread. From the disjunction comes the destruction of the conjunction originating the thread; by the action in the other thread, disjunction from the other thread is produced — this is one moment.

Then, at the very time when, from disjunction, the destruction of the thread-conjunction occurs, at that very time, from the destruction of conjunction, the destruction of the thread occurs; upon its destruction, the destruction of the disjunction with the other thread that was supported by it. Then there would be the undesirable consequence of non-production of subsequent disjunction,

due to the absence of causal disjunction. Then, in the case of an entity possessing conjunction with another region, there would be absence of conjunction, and therefore, due to the impossibility of an opposing quality, the action would persist for a long time; and if it inheres in an eternal substance, it would be eternal — this is the problem. How?

When an action arises in a <s>paramāṇu</s> (ultimate atom) that produces a <s>dvyaṇuka</s> (dyad) and produces disjunction from the other atom, at that very time an action also arises in the other atom. Then, at the very time when, from disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction that produces the substance occurs, at that very time, by the action in the other atom, disjunction between the <s>dvyaṇuka</s> and the atom is produced. Then, at the very time when, from disjunction, the destruction of the conjunction of <s>dvyaṇuka</s> and atom occurs, at that very time, from the destruction of conjunction, the destruction of the <s>dvyaṇuka</s> occurs.

Upon its destruction, the destruction of the disjunction between <s>dvyaṇuka</s> and atom that was supported by it. And therefore, due to the impossibility of an opposing quality, the action inherent in an eternal substance would be eternal.

Due to the disjunction between the thread and atom-parts, it is disjunction — there is no fault. From the destruction of the substrate, it is the disjunction of the thread itself that is destroyed, not the disjunction between thread and atom-parts. From this, a subsequent disjunction arises — like the disjunction of body and space from the disjunction of finger and space. At that very time, the action, having produced conjunction, is destroyed — there is no fault.

Alternatively, simultaneously with the production of the disjunction between atom-parts, an action arises in that very thread. Then, from the disjunction between atom-parts, there is the destruction of the conjunction that originates the thread; and by the action in the thread, disjunction from another thread is produced — this is one moment.

Then, from the destruction of conjunction, the destruction of the thread. From its destruction, the simultaneous destruction of both the disjunction and the action residing in it. Or, when there is a conjunction of thread and grass and no production of a substance, then by the method stated earlier, from the destruction of the substrate and from the conjunctions, the destruction of the disjunction between thread and grass.

Priority (<s>paratva</s>) and posteriority (<s>aparatva</s>) are the causes of the cognitions expressed by the terms 'prior' and 'posterior.' They are of two kinds: produced by direction (<s>dik</s>) and produced by time (<s>kāla</s>). Of these, that produced by direction gives rise to the cognition of spatial difference.

That produced by time gives rise to the cognition of difference in age. Here, the production of that which is produced by direction is described. How? When two masses situated in one direction have a greater or lesser number of conjoined conjunctions, taking the proximate one as the reference point for a single observer, the cognition arises regarding the non-proximate substrate of priority: 'this one is distant from that.'

Then, in dependence upon that cognition, from the conjunction with the farther region of direction, there is the production of priority. Likewise, taking the distant one as the reference point, the cognition arises regarding the other, the substrate of posteriority: 'this one is proximate to that.'
Then, in dependence upon that cognition, from the conjunction with the nearer region of direction, there is the production of posteriority. How also with those produced by time?

Of a young person and an old person, both present in time, not fixed in any particular direction or place, when there is the presence of grown beard, roughness, wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth — for a single observer, taking the young person as the reference point, a cognition of remoteness arises regarding the old person.

Then, in dependence upon that cognition, from the conjunction with the farther region of time, there is the production of priority. And taking the old person as the reference point, a cognition of proximity arises regarding the young one. Then, in dependence upon that cognition, from the conjunction with the nearer region of time, there is the production of posteriority.

The destruction, however, occurs from the destruction of the relative cognition, the conjunction, or the substance. From the destruction of the relative cognition first: when priority has been produced, at the time when the general cognition arises, then the relative cognition is being destroyed while the cognition of the quality of priority is being produced from the general cognition and its relations — this is one moment.

Then, the destruction of the relative cognition and the production of the quality-cognition. Then, from the destruction of the relative cognition, the quality is being destroyed while the substance-cognition is being produced from the quality-cognition and its relations — this is one moment. Then the production of the substance-cognition and the destruction of the quality.

How also from the destruction of conjunction? Simultaneously with the relative cognition, an action arises in the substrate of priority. By that action, disjunction from the directional mass is produced. From the relative cognition, the production of priority — this is one moment.

Then, the production of the general cognition and the destruction of the conjunction of the directional mass. Then, at the time when the quality-cognition arises, at that very time, from the destruction of the conjunction of the directional mass, the destruction of the quality. How also from the destruction of substance?

When an action has arisen in a part of the substrate of priority, at the very time it produces disjunction from another part, at that very time the relative cognition arises. Then, from the disjunction, at the very time there is destruction of conjunction, at that very time priority is produced. Then, from the destruction of conjunction, the destruction of substance; and from its destruction, the destruction of the quality residing in it.

How also from the simultaneous destruction of substance and relative cognition? When an action arises in a part of the substrate of priority, at that very time the relative cognition arises; and by the action, disjunction from another part is produced, and the production of priority — this is one moment.

Then, at the very time when from the part-disjunction there is destruction of the substance-originating conjunction, at that very time the general cognition arises. Thereupon, from the destruction of conjunction, the destruction of substance, and from the general cognition, the destruction of the relative cognition — this is one moment.
Then, from the destruction of substance and relative cognition, the destruction of priority. How also from the destruction of substance and conjunction?

When an action arisen in a part of the substrate of priority produces disjunction from another part, at that very time there is the simultaneous production of the mass-action and the relative cognition. Then, at the very time when priority is produced, at that very time from the disjunction there is destruction of the substance-originating conjunction, and by the mass-action, disjunction of the directional mass is produced, and the general cognition arises — this is one moment.

Then, at the very time when the general cognition arises, at that very time from the destruction of the substance-originating conjunction, the mass is destroyed, and from the destruction of the mass, the destruction of the mass-conjunction. Then, simultaneously with the quality-cognition, from the destruction of the mass-directional-mass conjunction, the destruction of priority.

How also from the simultaneous destruction of conjunction and relative cognition? When priority is produced, there is an action in the substrate of priority. Then, at the very time when the general cognition of priority arises, at that very time by the mass-action, disjunction of the directional mass is produced. Then, from the general cognition, the destruction of the relative cognition, and from the disjunction, the destruction of the directional-mass conjunction — this is one moment.
Then, from the destruction of the conjunction and relative cognition, the destruction of priority.

How also from the simultaneous destruction of all three — the inherent cause, the non-inherent cause, and the efficient cause? When the relative cognition arises, there is an action in a part of the mass. Then, at the very time when by that action disjunction from another part is produced and the relative cognition produces priority, at that very time there is also an action in the mass. Then from the part-disjunction, the destruction of the mass-originating conjunction, and by the mass-action, disjunction of the directional mass is produced, and the general cognition arises — this is one moment.

Then, from the destruction of conjunction, the destruction of the mass; from the disjunction, the destruction of the directional-mass conjunction; from the general cognition, the destruction of the relative cognition — all this is simultaneous. From the destruction of all three — the inherent cause, the non-inherent cause, and the efficient cause — the destruction of priority.
Cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), apprehension (<s>upalabdhi</s>), knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), and awareness (<s>pratyaya</s>) are synonyms.
It is of many kinds, due to the infinity of objects; and it is determined for each particular object.

Although it is of many varieties, in summary it is of two kinds: knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) and ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Of these, ignorance is fourfold, characterized by doubt, error, non-determination, and dream.

Doubt, first, arises from seeing merely the similarity between two well-known particulars, from the recollection of the distinguishing features of both, and from <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — it is a deliberation wavering between both, thinking 'which is it?'

It is of two kinds: internal and external. Internal doubt, first, arises regarding an oracle who, having declared correctly or incorrectly, then declares again — at all three times there is doubt: 'is it correct or incorrect?'
External doubt is of two kinds: regarding a perceptible object and regarding an imperceptible object.

Of these, regarding an imperceptible object first: from seeing a common mark, from the recollection of the distinguishing features of both, and from <s>adharma</s>, doubt arises. For example, in a forest, from seeing merely a horn: 'is it a cow or a wild ox?'

Regarding a perceptible object also: from seeing merely the similarity of uprightness between a post and a person, from the non-apprehension of distinguishing features such as crookedness, when the universal and particular of 'post-ness' and the like are not manifest — from the recollection of the distinguishing features of both, the cognition of the self, being drawn to both, wavers like a swing: 'is this indeed a post or a person?'
Error (<s>viparyaya</s>) also occurs only regarding objects of perception and inference.

Regarding a perceptible object first: between two well-known particulars, from incorrect perception by a sense organ afflicted by bile, phlegm, or wind, from the impressions born of knowledge of an object not present, in dependence upon the conjunction of self and mind and from <s>adharma</s> — the cognition 'this is that' where it is not — that is error.

As when one cognizes a horse in a cow. Even when perception is absent, there can be a conviction of perception, as when one perceives the autumn sky — free from dense cloud cover, resembling a motionless ocean, deep blue — as darkness, dark like a heap of collyrium powder.
Even in the domain of inference, one may infer fire from steam and the like, mistaking them for smoke; and from seeing the horns of a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox), one may cognize it as a cow.

In the doctrines of the <s>Śākyas</s> (Buddhists) and others, which are contrary to the teaching of the three <s>Vedas</s>, the false cognition 'this is the good' constitutes erroneous cognition (<s>viparyaya</s>). Also: the notion of self in the body, senses, and mind; the perception of permanence in what is produced; the cognition that an effect arises when the cause is deficient; the cognition 'this is harmful' when what is beneficial is taught; and the cognition 'this is beneficial' when what is harmful is taught.

Indeterminate cognition (<s>anadhyavasāya</s>) also arises in the domain of perception and inference. In the domain of perception: with regard to things whose nature is well-known or unknown, due to preoccupation or incapacity, there is mere apprehension without determinate judgment — that is indeterminate cognition.

For example, a person from <s>Bāhīka</s> (Punjab) has indeterminate cognition regarding the jackfruit and similar objects. In that case, the determinate judgment depends on existence (<s>sattā</s>), substanceness (<s>dravyatva</s>), earthness (<s>pṛthivītva</s>), treeness (<s>vṛkṣatva</s>), possession of color (<s>rūpavatva</s>), and so forth, as well as the perception of branches, and so on.

Even the universal 'jackfruit-ness' — which persists in jackfruits and is excluded from mangoes and the like — is itself perceptible; however, merely due to the absence of verbal instruction, no cognition of a specific name arises.
In the domain of inference too, a resident of the coconut island, from seeing only the dewlap, has the indeterminate cognition: 'What kind of creature could this be?'
The experience through the gateway of the senses alone, of one whose senses have ceased and whose mind has dissolved — that mental experience is dream-cognition (<s>svapnajñāna</s>). How?

When, by an effort arising from unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), prompted by the will-directed bodily activity of the self, for the purpose of rest at night and for the digestion of food of beings wearied during the day, the mind stands still and motionless in the inner heart-region, a non-sensory seat of the self, due to the connection between the self and the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), in the cessation of the continuous flow of mental activity — then it is called 'one whose mind has dissolved.'

When the mind has dissolved, the assemblage of senses ceases. In that state, with the continuous flow of the <s>prāṇa</s> and <s>apāna</s> breaths continuing, from a specific conjunction of the self and mind, from the <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression) called sleep, through the gateway of the senses alone, in the absence of actual sense objects, dream-cognition having the form of perception arises.
That is of three kinds: from the intensity of mental impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), from humoral disorder (<s>dhātudoṣa</s>), and from unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>).

Of these, from the intensity of mental impressions: when a person full of desire or anger falls asleep while thinking about a particular object with intense concentration, then that very stream of thought takes on the form of perception.

From humoral disorder: one of wind-constitution or one afflicted by wind sees flying through space and the like. One of bile-constitution or one afflicted by bile sees entering into fire, golden mountains, and the like.
One of phlegm-constitution or one afflicted by phlegm sees crossing rivers and oceans, snowy mountains, and the like.

What occurs regarding things experienced or not experienced, whether familiar or unfamiliar — whatever foretells good fortune, such as riding an elephant, obtaining an umbrella, and the like — all that arises from <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impressions) and <s>dharma</s> (merit). And the opposite — such as anointing with oil, riding a donkey, and the like — all that arises from <s>adharma</s> (demerit) and <s>saṃskāra</s>.
Regarding things entirely unfamiliar, it arises from <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit/demerit) alone.

Although the dream occurs when the assemblage of senses has ceased, still, since it is the review of the past stream of cognitions, it is merely a form of memory. Thus this fourfold cognition is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance/non-valid cognition).
<s>Vidyā</s> (valid cognition) is also fourfold: characterized as <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>laiṅgika</s> (inferential), <s>smṛti</s> (memory), and <s>ārṣa</s> (intuition of sages).
Of these, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception): that which arises depending on a sense organ (<s>akṣa</s>) is <s>pratyakṣa</s>.

The sense organs (<s>akṣas</s>) are six: smell (<s>ghrāṇa</s>), taste (<s>rasana</s>), sight (<s>cakṣus</s>), touch (<s>tvak</s>), hearing (<s>śrotra</s>), and mind (<s>manas</s>). It arises with regard to the categories of substance and so forth.

With regard to substance, firstly of two kinds: in large things, from the fourfold contact of substanceness in many substances, manifest color, and illumination; and with the auxiliary conditions of <s>dharma</s> and so forth — there is mere apprehension of the form.

From the contact of the self and mind, depending on the qualifiers of universal, particular, substance, quality, and action — perception arises: 'existent,' 'a substance,' 'earth,' 'having horns,' 'white,' 'a cow,' 'is going.'

In the case of color, taste, smell, and touch, from their inherence in multiple substances, from their own internal distinctions, and from contact with their own substratum, perception arises through its specific sense organ. By that very sense organ is the apprehension.

Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, fluidity, viscosity, velocity, and action — these, from their inherence in a perceptible substance, are grasped by sight and touch.

Cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and effort (<s>prayatna</s>) — these are apprehended from the conjunction of both the self and mind. Existence (<s>bhāva</s>), substanceness (<s>dravyatva</s>), qualityness (<s>guṇatva</s>), actionness (<s>karmatva</s>), and the like — being co-inherent with the apprehended substratum — are grasped by the sense organs that grasp the substratum. This is the perception of ordinary beings like us.

But for <s>yogins</s> (meditators) superior to us, who are in <s>yoga</s>, with mind assisted by <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>, there arises non-erroneous direct vision of the true nature of the self, inner space, direction, time, <s>paramāṇus</s> (atoms), wind, and mind, as well as of the qualities, actions, universals, and particulars inhering in them, and of inherence (<s>samavāya</s>).

For those who are disjoined from <s>yoga</s>, however, from the fourfold contact, through the power of the assistance of <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>, perception arises with regard to subtle, concealed, and remote objects.

Of these, the mere apprehension of the true nature of universals and particulars is the perceptual cognition that is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition); the <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) are the categories of substance and so forth; the <s>pramātṛ</s> (knower) is the self; the <s>pramiti</s> (resultant cognition) is the cognition having substance and other things as its object.

In the arising of the cognition of universals and particulars, the mere undifferentiated apprehension is the perceptual <s>pramāṇa</s>; in this, there is no other <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it does not have the nature of a result.

Alternatively, the cognition that arises from the fourfold contact regarding all categories — non-erroneous and non-verbal — that is the perceptual <s>pramāṇa</s>; the <s>prameyas</s> are the categories of substance and so forth; the <s>pramātṛ</s> is the self; the <s>pramiti</s> is the perception of qualities, faults, and neutrality.
That which arises from the perception of a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is <s>laiṅgika</s> (inferential cognition).
The logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>), moreover:
That which is connected with the thing to be inferred, and is well-established in what possesses the property of the inferable,
and which does not exist at all in the absence of that — that is the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>), the indicator of inference.
What is contrary to this, by one or two of these conditions,
is contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful — <s>Kāśyapa</s> declared it a non-mark (<s>aliṅga</s>).

That which co-occurs with the thing to be inferred in a particular place or particular time, and is well-established in all or some instances that possess the property of the inferable, and which is definitely absent through valid means of knowledge in everything that is the opposite of the inferable — that is the logical mark which indicates something whose nature is not directly established.

The positive example: wherever there is smoke, there is fire; in the absence of fire, smoke also does not exist. Thus, for one whose convention is well-established, from the undoubted perception of smoke, from the recollection of the co-occurrence, the subsequent determination of fire follows.

Thus everywhere, the logical mark of one thing is that which is inseparable from it in place and time. In the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise), the mention of 'effect and the like' is for the purpose of illustration, not of restriction — because co-occurrence is seen from a single observation.

For example: the <s>adhvaryu</s> (priest) chanting '<s>oṃ śrāvaya</s>' is the logical mark of the concealed <s>hotṛ</s> (priest); the rising of the moon is the mark of the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the night-lotus; in autumn, the clearing of the waters is the mark of the rising of <s>Agastya</s> (the star Canopus).

All such cases are established by the mere statement of connection 'this belongs to that.' It is of two kinds: <s>dṛṣṭa</s> (based on what is seen) and <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> (based on what is generally observed).

Of these, <s>dṛṣṭa</s> is inference where the well-known and the thing to be established are of absolutely the same universal class. For example, having observed only the dewlap in a cow, from seeing the dewlap in another place too, one cognizes it as a cow.

<s>Sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> is inference where the well-known and the thing to be established differ absolutely in universal class, but the inference proceeds from the continuation of the common property between the logical mark and the thing inferred.

For example, having observed that the activities of farmers, merchants, and royal servants are fruitful, one infers fruit for the activities of those following the <s>varṇāśrama</s> (caste and stage of life) system, who act without any visible purpose.

In this, the perception of the logical mark is the <s>pramāṇa</s>; the <s>pramiti</s> is the cognition of fire. Alternatively, the cognition of fire itself is the <s>pramāṇa</s>; and the <s>pramiti</s> is the perception of qualities, faults, and neutrality in fire. This inference has its own ascertained object.
Verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) and the other means of cognition are also included within inference, due to their having the same method.

Just as, for one whose convention is well-established, inference arises regarding a supersensory object from the perception of an undoubted logical mark and the recollection of the well-established co-occurrence — even so, it arises from verbal testimony and other sources.

The <s>Āmnāya</s> (scripture), which is characterized by <s>śruti</s> (revelation) and <s>smṛti</s> (tradition), also depends on the authority of its speaker. Because its authority is declared by his word: 'The authority of the <s>Āmnāya</s> is from inference, and non-eternal; creation of sentences in the <s>Veda</s> is preceded by intelligence; giving is preceded by intelligence' — this has been stated.
From the observation that comprehension occurs through the gesture of one whose signs are well-known, that too is indeed inference.
Because of the explanation of the unfamiliar <s>gavaya</s> (a wild ox) by means of the cow by a trustworthy person, <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) is nothing but trustworthy testimony.
<s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption), being contradictory from the visible evidence, is itself inference, being what is inferred from hearing.
<s>Sambhava</s> (inclusion) is also inference alone, due to the relationship of invariable concomitance.
<s>Abhāva</s> (absence) is also inference alone. Just as an arisen effect is the mark of the existence of its cause, so too a non-arisen effect is the mark of the non-existence of its cause.
Likewise, <s>aitihya</s> (tradition) also, being non-false, is nothing but the instruction of a trustworthy person.

<s>Parārthānumāna</s> (inference for the sake of others) is the communication of one's own ascertained meaning through a statement of five members.
