The communication of one's own ascertained meaning to others who are in doubt, have false notions, or are uninstructed, through a statement of exactly five members, should be understood as <s>parārthānumāna</s>.
The members are: <s>pratijñā</s> (proposition), <s>apadeśa</s> (statement of the reason), <s>nidarśana</s> (example), <s>anusandhāna</s> (application), and <s>pratyāmnāya</s> (restatement).
The non-contradictory indication of the subject to be inferred is the <s>pratijñā</s> (proposition).

The <s>pratijñā</s> (proposition) is merely an indication, meant to bring the subject (<s>dharmin</s>), qualified by the property to be established, within the range of instruction. For example: 'Wind is a substance.'
By the inclusion of 'non-contradictory,' those that contradict perception, inference, accepted scripture, or one's own statement are excluded.

For example: 'Fire is not hot' contradicts perception. 'Space is dense' contradicts inference. 'A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should drink liquor' contradicts scripture. When a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> says 'the effect pre-exists in the cause,' it contradicts his own doctrine. 'Sound does not convey meaning' contradicts one's own statement.

The statement of the logical mark is the <s>apadeśa</s> (reason). That which is concomitant with the subject to be inferred, universally established through a universal in all things of the same class, and absent in everything of the opposite class — that is called the logical mark. The statement of that is the <s>apadeśa</s>.

For example: 'Because it possesses action and possesses qualities.' And thus, in the subject to be inferred, and in everything of the same class, there is possession of qualities; and in everything there is not possession of action.
Both of these are completely absent in non-substances. Therefore, the statement of that is established as the <s>apadeśa</s> (reason).

By this, the pseudo-reasons — the unestablished, contradictory, doubtful, and inconclusive statements — are rejected. Of these, the unestablished is of four kinds: unestablished for both parties, unestablished for one party, unestablished in the state of the subject, and unestablished in the subject to be inferred.
Unestablished for both parties is one that is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent. For example: 'Sound is eternal because it has parts.'

Unestablished for one party is, for example: 'Sound is eternal because it is produced.' Unestablished in the state of the subject is when, for the purpose of ascertaining fire through the state of smoke, smoke is presented in mist — unestablished because the state of smoke is not present.

Unestablished in the subject to be inferred is, for example: 'Darkness is an earthy substance because it possesses dark color.' That which, though not present in the subject to be inferred, is present in everything of the same class and absent in everything of the opposite class — that, establishing the opposite, is contradictory. For example: 'Because it has horns, therefore it is a horse.'

But that which, being present in the subject, is common to both the same class and the different class — that, being a generator of doubt, is doubtful. For example: 'Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow.' And some say that when two reasons having the stated characteristics, being mutually contradictory, occur together in a single subject, since we observe doubt arising, this is another kind of doubtful reason.
For example: the possession of action and the non-possession of touch, with respect to whether the mind is corporeal or incorporeal.

But this is in fact an uncommon reason — like being inaudible and being perceptible — because the possibility of either side is excluded when the two are combined. Hence we shall say it is inconclusive.
But in the treatise, it is indicated here and there that observation of both alternatives is the cause of doubt. No; doubt does not arise from the observation of two objects.

The observation of two objects is a cause in the production of doubt; but when the two are of equal strength, from their mutual contradiction, there would be non-production of determination, not the causation of doubt. And there is no equal strength of those two, since one of them — the indication of the subject — is invalidated by scripture. This, however, is just a variety of the contradictory.

And that which, being present in the subject, is absent in both the same class and the different class — that is unestablished for one party and, being a cause of non-ascertainment, is inconclusive. For example: 'The effect pre-exists because of production.'
This is restricted by the statement that an unestablished thing is not a valid reason.

But this particular characteristic has been declared a cause of doubt in the treatise: 'Because a particular characteristic, in things of the same class that are different entities, is seen in both ways.' Not so, because it has a different meaning — because the characteristic is seen in sound.

When it is said that doubt does not arise, this particular characteristic would not be a distinguishing feature of any one of the substances and so forth — audibility would in fact turn out to be a universal. Why? Because it is said: 'Because a particular characteristic, in things of the same class that are different entities — that is, among the divisions of substance and so forth — is seen of each individual characteristic in both ways.' This is not a cause of doubt; otherwise, doubt would arise regarding all six categories. Therefore, doubt arises from the cognition of a universal alone.

The <s>nidarśana</s> (example) is of two kinds: through similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) and through dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>). Of these, the observation of the logical mark following the universal of the subject to be inferred through the universal — that is the example through similarity.

For example: 'Whatever possesses action is seen to be a substance, like an arrow.' And the observation of the absence of the logical mark in the opposite of the subject to be inferred — that is the example through dissimilarity. For example: 'Whatever is not a substance does not possess action, like existence (<s>sattā</s>).'
By this, pseudo-examples are rejected.

Such as: 'Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is incorporeal is seen to be eternal, like an atom, like an action, like a pot, like darkness, like space' — and 'whatever is a substance possesses action' — these are pseudo-examples through similarity: being unestablished in the mark, in the subject, or in both; lacking the common property; and having the wrong common property.

'Whatever is non-eternal is corporeal, like an action, like an atom, like space, like darkness, like a pot; whatever is inactive is a non-substance' — these are pseudo-examples through dissimilarity: being non-excluded from the mark, from the subject, or from both; unestablished in the substratum; non-excluded; and having the wrong exclusion.
In the example, the application (<s>anusandhāna</s>) is the connecting of the logical mark, which was seen together with the universal of the subject to be inferred, to the subject to be inferred.

The logical mark, which is universal and has been stated as having the character of the property of the subject to be inferred, whose power has not yet been perceived, and which was seen together with the universal of the established property in the example — the statement by which it is connected to the subject to be inferred is the <s>anusandhāna</s> (application). Accordingly: 'Wind possesses action.'
And in the absence of the subject to be inferred, perceiving its non-existence: 'And wind is not so — not without action.'

The restatement of the proposition for the purpose of establishing certainty in others, when the subject indicated as what is to be inferred is not yet settled, is the <s>pratyāmnāya</s> (restatement/conclusion).

The restatement of the proposition, for the purpose of establishing certainty in others — through the complete statement whose parts (reason and so forth) have empowered it — when the subject indicated as what is to be established is not yet settled, is the <s>pratyāmnāya</s> (restatement). Thus: 'Therefore it is indeed a substance.'

For, in the absence of this, neither the other members collectively nor individually have the capacity to convey that meaning. If one objects that the meaning is already understood, and therefore [the restatement is unnecessary] — no, because of over-extension.

For then, immediately after the proposition, the mere statement of the reason alone should be made, since for the learned, from the recollection of positive and negative concomitance, the understanding of the meaning will follow. Therefore, the completion of the meaning is right here.
How? By 'Sound is non-eternal,' sound, qualified only by unsettled non-eternality, is stated. By 'because it is produced by effort,' only the property that proves non-eternality is stated.
By 'Whatever is produced by effort is seen to be non-eternal, like a pot,' only the following of the universal of the proof by the universal of the thing to be proved is stated.
By 'Whatever is eternal is seen to be not produced by effort, like space,' the non-existence of the proof-property in the absence of the property to be proved is demonstrated.

And thus, sound is observed to be immediately preceded by effort, but is not observed to be not preceded by effort, like space. Through the methods of co-presence (<s>anvaya</s>) and co-absence (<s>vyatireka</s>), the connection of the probative general [property] possessing the observed capacity to [prove] sound is understood. Therefore, sound is non-eternal. By this, the completion of the intended meaning — that sound is indeed non-eternal — is understood. Therefore, through a statement of five members alone, the communication of one's ascertained meaning to others is accomplished. Thus, inference for the sake of others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) is established.

Ascertaining knowledge born from the perception of a distinguishing feature, which opposes doubt, is <s>nirṇaya</s> (determination). This is either perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) or inference (<s>anumāna</s>).
That which arises from the perception of a distinguishing feature and opposes doubt is perceptual determination.

For example, when doubt arises from seeing the mere similarity in uprightness between a post and a person — 'Is this a post or a person?' — due to the recollection of the distinguishing features of both while the distinguishing features are not [yet] perceived, then from the perception of the head, hands, and the like, the ascertaining knowledge 'this is indeed a person' is a perceptual determination.

When doubt arises from seeing mere horns — 'Is this a cow or a wild ox (<s>gavaya</s>)?' — then from the mere perception of a dewlap, the ascertaining knowledge 'this is indeed a cow' is an inferential determination.

Arising from a specific conjunction of the <s>ātman</s> and mind, which depends on the perception of a mark, desire, recollection, and so forth, and from a <s>saṃskāra</s> (mental impression) produced by sharpness, practice, respect, and cognition — with regard to objects seen, heard, or experienced — memory (<s>smṛti</s>), which has past objects as its domain, is the cause of residual ascertainment, desire, recollection, and aversion.

For the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages) who are the authors of the sacred tradition (<s>āmnāya</s>), the knowledge that arises regarding past, future, and present objects that are beyond the senses — such as <s>dharma</s> and the rest — whether contained in texts or not contained in texts, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind and from a specific <s>dharma</s> — that intuitive knowledge which conveys the objects as they truly are, is called <s>ārṣa</s> (seer's knowledge).
That, in succession, belongs to divine <s>ṛṣis</s> sometimes, and to worldly persons as well — as when a girl says: 'Tomorrow my brother will come; my heart tells me so.'

The perception of <s>siddhas</s> (accomplished ones) is not a distinct kind of knowledge. Why? Because the perception by those who have achieved accomplishments through collyrium, foot-ointment, sword, pill, and the like — who are visible seers — of objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant, is perception itself.

Now, if the perception of the consequences of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> for celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial beings, caused by the planets, stars, constellations, and the like, is intended — that too is inference alone.

And if perception regarding <s>dharma</s> and the rest, independent of a logical mark, is intended — that too is included in either perception or seer's knowledge. Thus cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) [is explained].

Pleasure (<s>sukha</s>) is characterized by gratification. When a desired object such as a garland and the like is present, from the contact of the sense organ with the desired object, depending on <s>dharma</s> and the like, from a specific conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, there arises that which produces gratification, attachment, brightening of the eyes, and the like — that is pleasure.

With regard to past objects, it arises from memory. With regard to future objects, it arises from imagination (<s>saṅkalpa</s>). But the [pleasure] that manifests for the learned in the absence of recollection, desire, and imagination regarding objects — that is caused by knowledge, tranquility, contentment, and a specific <s>dharma</s>.
Pain (<s>duḥkha</s>) is characterized by affliction.

When an undesired object such as poison and the like is present, from the contact of the sense organ with the undesired object, depending on <s>adharma</s> and the like, from a specific conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, there arises that which causes resentment, affliction, and wretchedness — that is pain.
With regard to past objects such as snakes, tigers, thieves, and the like, it arises from memory. With regard to future objects, it arises from imagination.

Desire (<s>icchā</s>) is the longing for an unattained thing, whether for oneself or for another. It arises from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, depending on pleasure and the like, or depending on memory.

It is caused by effort, memory, <s>dharma</s>, and <s>adharma</s>. <s>Kāma</s> (lust), <s>abhilāṣa</s> (craving), <s>rāga</s> (passion), <s>saṅkalpa</s> (intention), <s>kāruṇya</s> (compassion), <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion), <s>upadhā</s> (deceit), <s>bhāva</s> (hidden intention) — these and others are varieties of desire. The desire for sexual union is <s>kāma</s>.

The desire for eating is <s>abhilāṣa</s> (craving). The desire for repeatedly enjoying objects is <s>rāga</s> (passion). The desire for an action not yet near is <s>saṅkalpa</s> (intention). The desire to remove another's suffering without regard for one's own interest is <s>kāruṇya</s> (compassion).

The desire to abandon objects upon seeing their faults is <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion). The desire to deceive others is <s>upadhā</s> (deceit). Desire concealed within is <s>bhāva</s> (hidden intention). From the distinction of actions such as 'wishing to do' and 'wishing to take away,' there are distinctions of desire.

<s>Dveṣa</s> (aversion) has the nature of burning. That in the presence of which one considers oneself to be as if burning — that is aversion. It arises from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, depending on pain or depending on memory.

It is caused by effort, memory, <s>dharma</s>, and <s>adharma</s>. <s>Krodha</s> (anger), <s>droha</s> (malice), <s>manyu</s> (wrath), <s>akṣama</s> (intolerance), and <s>āmarṣa</s> (indignation) are varieties of aversion.

Effort (<s>prayatna</s>): exertion (<s>saṃrambha</s>) and enthusiasm (<s>utsāha</s>) are its synonyms. It is of two kinds: preceded by vital force (<s>jīvana</s>) and preceded by desire and aversion. Of these, that preceded by vital force is the impeller of the continuity of inhalation and exhalation during sleep, and at the time of awakening it is the cause of the internal organ reaching the other sense organs.

The origination of this [effort] preceded by vital force is from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, depending on <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. The other [kind], however, is the cause of the activity that is capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and sustains the body.
It arises from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, depending on desire or depending on aversion.

<s>Gurutva</s> (heaviness) is the cause of the downward motion of water and earth. It is imperceptible, inferable from downward motion, and opposed by conjunction, effort, and <s>saṃskāra</s>. Its determinations as eternal and non-eternal, beginning from atoms, are like those of color.

<s>Dravatva</s> (fluidity) is the cause of flowing motion. It resides in three substances. It is of two kinds: natural (<s>sāṃsiddhika</s>) and occasioned (<s>naimittika</s>). The natural is a specific quality of water. The occasioned is a common quality of earth and fire.

The determinations of the natural [fluidity] as eternal and non-eternal are like those of heaviness. If one objects that the natural [fluidity] is contradicted by the observation of solidification [of water] — no.

The conjunction of water-atoms that are combined with celestial fire with each other — the substance-producing [conjunction] called solidification — through that, due to the obstruction of the fluidity of the atoms, there is no occurrence of fluidity in the effect such as ice, hail, and the like.
The occasioned [fluidity] of earth and fire is produced by contact with fire.

How? In the case of ghee, lac, honey, beeswax, and the like, when action arises in the causal atoms from contact with fire, depending on impetus, and from the disjunctions produced by those [actions] comes the destruction of the substance-producing conjunction, and upon the cessation of the effect-substance, fluidity arises in the independent atoms from heat depending on contact with fire. Then, in those [atoms], from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and atom depending on the unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) of the enjoyers, when action arises, from the conjunctions produced by those [actions], through the sequence of dyads and so forth, an effect-substance is produced. And in that [substance], simultaneously with the arising of color and the like, fluidity is produced through the sequence of causal qualities.
<s>Sneha</s> (viscosity) is a specific quality of water. It is the cause of cohesion, polishing, and the like. Its determinations as eternal and non-eternal are like those of heaviness.

<s>Saṃskāra</s> (dispositional force) is of three kinds: <s>vega</s> (velocity), <s>bhāvanā</s> (mental impression), and <s>sthitisthāpaka</s> (elasticity). Among these, <s>vega</s> arises in the five corporeal substances from <s>karma</s> (action) dependent on specific causes; it is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a determinate direction, is opposed to the contact of a specific substance possessing <s>sparśa</s> (touch), and in some cases arises in accordance with the prior order of qualities of the cause. The one designated <s>bhāvanā</s>, however, is a quality of the <s>ātman</s> (self) and is the cause of <s>smṛti</s> (memory) and <s>pratyabhijñāna</s> (recognition) regarding objects seen, heard, or experienced; it inheres in that which possesses <s>jñāna</s> (cognition) and is opposed to non-suffering and the like. It is born from keenness, repetition, and attentiveness of cognition. From the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> (mind) dependent on a keen cognition, an extraordinary <s>saṃskāra</s> arises with respect to a wondrous object — as, for example, when a southerner sees a camel. When disciplines such as learning, crafts, physical exercises, and the like are practiced repeatedly, from each successive cognition regarding that very same object, dependent upon each preceding <s>saṃskāra</s>, an extraordinary <s>saṃskāra</s> arises from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>. When one fixes the <s>manas</s> on the eye through effort and desires to see an unprecedented object — like the sight of a flash of lightning — an attentive cognition arises, and dependent upon it, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, an extraordinary <s>saṃskāra</s> arises — as, for example, from seeing golden and silver lotuses in <s>Devahrada</s>. <s>Sthitisthāpaka</s> (elasticity), however, abiding in substances possessing <s>sparśa</s> (touch), in those characterized by a particular arrangement of dense parts and enduring over a period of time, restores its substratum, when altered, to its original state. Its effect is observed in modifications of stationary and moving things — in bows, branches, horns, tusks, bones, threads, cloths, and the like — when they are bent or twisted. Its production as eternal and non-eternal is like that of <s>gurutva</s> (gravity).

<s>Dharma</s> (merit) is a quality of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person). It is the cause of what is pleasing, beneficial, and conducive to <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) for the agent; it is beyond the senses, opposed to the cognition of ultimate suffering, and arises from the conjunction of the person's inner faculty with a purified intention; it has specific means prescribed for those belonging to the <s>varṇas</s> (social classes) and <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life). Its means, prescribed in <s>Śruti</s> (revealed scripture) and <s>Smṛti</s> (traditional texts), are substances, qualities, and actions established as general and specific for those belonging to the <s>varṇas</s> and <s>āśramas</s>. Among these, the general means of <s>dharma</s> are: faith, non-violence, benevolence toward beings, truthful speech, non-stealing, celibacy, sincerity, abandonment of anger, ritual bathing, use of purifying substances, devotion to the chosen deity, fasting, and vigilance. For <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, <s>Kṣatriyas</s>, and <s>Vaiśyas</s>, the common duties are sacrifice, study, and giving; the specific duties of a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> are accepting gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices, along with the <s>saṃskāras</s> (sacramental rites) prescribed for his class. For a <s>Kṣatriya</s>, the duties are proper protection of subjects, punishment of the wicked, not turning back in battle, and the <s>saṃskāras</s> specific to his class. For a <s>Vaiśya</s>, the duties are trade, agriculture, and cattle-rearing, along with the <s>saṃskāras</s> specific to his class. For a <s>Śūdra</s>, the duty is service to the higher classes and ritual acts performed without mantras. For those in the <s>āśramas</s>, the <s>brahmacārin</s> (celibate student) dwelling in the teacher's house is to perform duties prescribed by his own scripture: service to the teacher, tending the sacred fire, and going on alms-rounds, as well as abstaining from honey, meat, sleeping during the day, applying collyrium, anointing the body, and the like.

For the householder (<s>gṛhastha</s>) who has completed his studies and vows and taken a wife, the daily performance, morning and evening, of the five great sacrifices (<s>mahāyajñas</s>) called <s>bhūta</s>, <s>manuṣya</s>, <s>deva</s>, <s>pitṛ</s>, and <s>brahma</s> — with wealth acquired through the modes of livelihood called <s>śālīna</s> (gleaning) and <s>yāyāvara</s> (wandering) — along with the regular <s>pākayajña</s> rites performed with a single fire, and when capacity permits, the <s>haviryajña</s> rites beginning with <s>agnyādheya</s> and the <s>somayajña</s> rites beginning with <s>agniṣṭoma</s>. Celibacy during the intervening seasons, and the begetting of offspring. For one who has departed from the village, whether a <s>brahmacārin</s> or a householder, forest-dwelling and the wearing of bark garments, deer-skin, and the keeping of hair, beard, nails, and body-hair uncut. For the forest-dweller (<s>vānaprastha</s>), eating only what remains after offering the forest oblation and feeding guests. For one who has faith and has adopted any one of the three previous stages, having given the assurance of safety to all beings at all times and renounced his own ritual actions, being vigilant in <s>yama</s> (restraints) and <s>niyama</s> (observances), the practice of <s>yoga</s> through the contemplation of the six <s>padārthas</s> (categories) — this is the way of the renunciant (<s>pravrajita</s>). Without aiming at any visible purpose, these means, together with purity of disposition, give rise to <s>dharma</s> from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>.

<s>Adharma</s> (demerit) is also a quality of the <s>ātman</s> (self). It is the cause of what is harmful and leads to retribution for the agent; it is beyond the senses and opposed to the cognition of ultimate suffering. Its means are those prohibited in the scriptures and contrary to the means of <s>dharma</s> — violence, falsehood, theft, and the like — as well as the non-performance of prescribed duties and negligence. Dependent upon an impure intention, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, <s>adharma</s> arises.

For the unwise person who possesses attachment and aversion, from predominant <s>dharma</s> accompanied by a small amount of <s>adharma</s>, arising from the propelling force, there is conjunction with desirable bodies, senses, objects, pleasures, and the like in the worlds of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Indra</s>, <s>Prajāpati</s>, the <s>Pitṛs</s> (ancestors), and humans, in accordance with one's dispositions. Likewise, from predominant <s>adharma</s> accompanied by a small amount of <s>dharma</s>, there is conjunction with undesirable bodies, senses, objects, and sufferings in the realms of <s>pretas</s> (departed spirits) and <s>tiryak</s> (animals).

Thus, from <s>dharma</s> characterized by activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), accompanied by <s>adharma</s>, there is the bondage of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) again and again among gods, humans, animals, and hell-beings.

However, for one who has been born in a pure family, whose actions were preceded by knowledge and performed without desire for their fruits, who desires to know the means of cessation of suffering, who has approached a teacher and attained true knowledge of the six <s>padārthas</s> (categories), upon the cessation of ignorance, being free from passion — due to the absence of attachment, aversion, and the like, and consequently the non-arising of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> born from them, and upon the exhaustion through experience of those previously accumulated — having experienced the happiness of contentment and the dissolution of the body, upon the cessation of attachment and the rest, <s>dharma</s> characterized by cessation (<s>nivṛtti</s>), being pure, produces the happiness born of the vision of ultimate reality and then ceases. Then, due to the cessation of the seed, there is the dissolution of <s>manas</s>, body, and the rest; upon the non-arising of body and the rest again, the quiescence like a fire whose fuel is consumed — this is <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).

<s>Śabda</s> (sound) is a quality of <s>ambara</s> (ether), apprehended by the ear, momentary, opposed to both its effect and its cause, produced from conjunction, disjunction, or another <s>śabda</s>, located in a limited region, and having causes both of the same and different kinds. It is of two kinds: that characterized as <s>varṇa</s> (articulate sound) and that characterized as <s>dhvani</s> (inarticulate sound). Among these, that characterized as <s>varṇa</s> begins with the letter 'a' and so forth, and that characterized as <s>dhvani</s> is caused by conches and the like. Regarding the production of <s>varṇa</s>: from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, dependent on memory, there arises the desire to utter a <s>varṇa</s>; thereupon effort arises; dependent on that, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and <s>vāyu</s> (air), action arises in the air; and that air, moving upward, strikes the throat and other places of articulation; then, dependent on the conjunction of the air at the place of articulation, from the conjunction of that place with <s>ākāśa</s> (space), <s>varṇa</s> is produced.

The non-articulate sound (<s>dhvani</s>) is also produced from the conjunction of the drum-skin with <s>ākāśa</s> (space), dependent on the conjunction of the drum with the drumstick. And from the disjunction of the sections of a bamboo flute, from the disjunction of the bamboo and <s>ākāśa</s>, and from a prior <s>śabda</s> (sound) produced by conjunction and disjunction, there arises a series of sounds like a series of waves. The apprehension occurs when it reaches the region of the ear through this series. Since there is no going or coming of either the ear or the sound, there is no apprehension of what has not arrived; therefore, the existence of the series is established by the method of residues.
In the <s>Praśastapādabhāṣya</s>, the category of <s>guṇa</s> (quality) is concluded.
Now begins the examination of the category of <s>karma</s> (action).

The five — <s>utkṣepaṇa</s> (upward movement), and the rest — all share the relation of <s>karmatva</s> (action-ness). Their common properties are: inhering in a single substance, being momentary, abiding in corporeal substances, being devoid of qualities, being produced from <s>gurutva</s> (gravity), <s>dravatva</s> (fluidity), <s>prayatna</s> (effort), or <s>samyoga</s> (conjunction), being opposed to the conjunction that is their own effect, being a cause that does not depend on conjunction or disjunction, being a non-inherent cause, being a producer of effects inhering in one's own and another's substratum, not producing things of the same kind, not producing substances, and possessing a determinate universal. The distinguishing feature is that each produces effects in a specific direction.

Among these, <s>utkṣepaṇa</s> (upward movement) is that action which arises in the parts of the body and in things connected with them, which is the cause of conjunction with spatial points in the upper direction and the cause of disjunction from spatial points in the lower direction, and which is produced from <s>gurutva</s> (gravity), <s>prayatna</s> (effort), and <s>samyoga</s> (conjunction) — that is <s>utkṣepaṇa</s>.
The action that causes conjunction and disjunction in the opposite manner is <s>apakṣepaṇa</s> (downward movement).

<s>Ākuñcana</s> (contraction) is that action by which the tip-parts of a straight substance undergo disjunction from their original positions and conjunction with the positions near the base, so that the composite substance becomes curved.
<s>Prasāraṇa</s> (expansion) is that action by which, through conjunction and disjunction occurring in the reverse manner, the composite substance becomes straight.
<s>Gamana</s> (general motion) is that action which causes conjunction with and disjunction from spatial points in no determinate direction.

This fivefold action too, when present in the parts of the body and in things connected to it, has a known cause; and what has an unknown cause — that is without a cause; and in those other things, that is movement.
The fivefold classification of actions by universal is unjustified, because there is no distinction in movement. For all momentary action, being merely movement, having arisen, produces conjunction and disjunction of its substrate with spatial regions above, below, or sideways by even the minutest extent — everywhere the cognition of movement is present; therefore all action is just movement.
No — because we observe the persistence and exclusion of cognitions class by class: 'here it is throwing upward, there it is throwing downward' — in this way, since the class-wise persistence and exclusion of cognitions is observed everywhere, the distinguishing ground of universals and particulars is understood.
From the distinguishing prefixes 'ud-' etc., and because each initiates an effect in a particular direction, the distinction of characterization is also established.
Even so, the restriction to 'only five' is untenable. Because in exiting, entering, and so forth too, class-wise persistence and exclusion of cognitions is observed.
If in throwing upward and so forth, because class-wise persistence and exclusion of cognitions is observed everywhere, a distinction of universal is accepted — then the same should apply to exiting, entering, and so forth.
If it is said that in those cases the persistence and exclusion of cognitions is due to difference of effect — no, because in throwing upward and so forth too, there would be the same consequence of persistence and exclusion from difference of effect alone.
But when the class-wise persistence and exclusion of cognitions is equally present, what is the special reason that only throwing upward and the rest have distinct universals but not exiting and the rest? There is none — because the consequence of confusion of universals would follow.
If exiting and the rest had distinct universals, confusion of universals would follow. How? Two observers see someone going from one room to another — they simultaneously have the cognitions of exiting and entering. Likewise, when one is at the doorway: 'he is entering' and 'he is exiting.'
But when the curtain etc. has been removed, there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of exiting, but only the cognition of movement.
Likewise, when a bamboo leaf etc. falls in a tube, many observers simultaneously have the cognitions of rotation, falling, and entering — hence the consequence of confusion of universals.
But no such confusion of cognitions is observed in throwing upward and the rest. Therefore, in throwing upward and the rest, the persistence and exclusion of cognitions is due to distinction of universals; but in exiting and the rest, it is due to distinction of effects.
How can there be simultaneous difference of cognition? If it is thought that just as there is no confusion of universals, so there is no multiple action in one thing — and thus how can there simultaneously be cognitions of rotation, falling, and entering in one action? — to that we reply: it is not so, because of the difference of directionally-specific conjunctions and disjunctions of parts and wholes.

For the observer who sees the conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts with spatial regions successively from the sides has the cognition of rotation. The one who observes disjunction from upper regions and conjunction below in the whole has the cognition of falling. The one who sees conjunction in the interior space of a tube and disjunction in the exterior space has the cognition of entering. Thus it is established that the difference of cognitions in exiting and the rest is due to difference of effects.
Let there be a distinction of universals for throwing upward and the rest, and for exiting and the rest a difference due to effects.

Now, is 'movement-ness' (<s>gamanatva</s>) a synonym of 'action-ness' (<s>karmatva</s>), or is it a different universal?
Whence your doubt?
Because the cognition of movement is undifferentiated from the cognition of action equally in throwing upward and the rest, it is understood to be a synonym of action-ness.
But since it is designated by a specific term like throwing upward and the rest, it might be a different universal.
No. Because it is synonymous with action-ness. Just as 'self-ness' (<s>ātmatva</s>) and 'person-ness' (<s>puruṣatva</s>) are synonyms, movement-ness is merely a synonym of action-ness.
Then why was the term 'movement' used with a specific designation? Because it serves to include rotation and the rest. The term 'movement' was used to include rotation, falling, vibration, and the rest, which were not included by the terms 'throwing upward' and the rest.
Otherwise, the very four that were stated with specific designations would become the objects of both the universal and specific designations.
Alternatively, let movement-ness be a different universal — it occurs only in rotation and the rest, which cause conjunction and disjunction with indefinite directions and places; and the word 'movement' should be understood as figurative when applied to throwing upward and the rest, due to the commonality of being the agent of conjunction and disjunction in their substrates.

The method of action with a known cause:
How? In desired activities such as sacrifice, study, giving, agriculture, and so forth, when one wishes to raise the hand upward or throw it downward, effort (<s>prayatna</s>) arises in a region of the self connected with the hand. From the conjunction of self and hand, regarding that effort and also gravity, action arises in the hand. As with the hand, so with all parts of the body — feet and so forth — and in the body as a whole.
How also in connected things? When one grasps a pestle with the hand and forms the desire 'I shall raise the pestle with my hand,' thereupon effort arises. Regarding that effort, from the conjunction of self and hand, at the very time when the action of throwing upward arises in the hand, at that very time, regarding that same effort, from the conjunction of hand and pestle, action arises in the pestle also.

Then, when the pestle has been thrown far upward, the desire for that purpose ceases, and again the desire to throw it down arises. Thereupon effort arises, and regarding that effort, from the conjunction as stated, simultaneously actions of throwing downward arise in the hand and pestle. Then, by the final action of the pestle, a conjunction called 'impact' is produced between the mortar and pestle. That conjunction, regarding the momentum (<s>vega</s>) residing in the pestle, produces in the pestle a causeless action of bouncing up.
That action, dependent on the impact, produces an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) in the pestle. Regarding that impression, the conjunction of pestle and hand produces a causeless bouncing action even in the struck object.
Although the prior impression may have been destroyed, still the conjunction of pestle and mortar, being of a particular kind capable of producing sharp action, is competent as an auxiliary in producing the impression.
Alternatively, the prior sharp impression, not being destroyed by the impact, remains. Therefore, there is no production of a further impression in what already possesses an impression. Hence, at the very time when a causeless bouncing action arises in the pestle depending on the impression and the impact, at that very time, regarding that same impression, from the conjunction of pestle and hand, a causeless bouncing action arises in the hand also.

The method of movement in thrown objects:
How? When one grasps a javelin with the hand and the desire to throw it upward arises, thereupon effort arises. Regarding that effort, from the two conjunctions as stated, simultaneous pulling actions arise in the javelin and hand.
When the hand is extended, the effort for that pulling ceases. Thereupon the desire arises: 'I shall throw it sideways, upward, far, or near.' Then effort conforming to that desire arises, and the conjunction of javelin and hand called 'pushing' (<s>nodana</s>) — from that, action arises in the javelin, and dependent on the pushing, produces an impression in it. Then, from the impression and the pushing, actions continue as long as there is no disjunction between hand and javelin. After the disjunction, when the pushing has ceased, from the impression alone, actions conforming to the effort arise upward, sideways, far, or near, until the falling.

Likewise, the procedure of motion in [the case of] a mechanical device. How? A strong man who has practiced, bracing the bow with his left hand and nocking an arrow with his right, having grasped the bowstring with the arrow in his fist, generates the desire to draw: 'I shall draw this strung bow.' Immediately after that, effort arises; from the conjunction of ātman and hand, which depends on that effort, pulling action arises in the hand at the very moment; at that very moment, from the conjunction of hand, bowstring, and arrow, which depends on that same effort, action arises in the bowstring and in the arrow; and from the two conjunctions at the tips of the bow, which depend on the conjunction of hand-bowstring-arrow qualified by effort, two actions arise at the tips of the bow — all this simultaneously. Thus, when the bow has been drawn to the ear, the knowledge arises that 'it should not be drawn further than this,' whence comes the destruction of the effort for the purpose of drawing. Then the desire to release arises. Immediately after that, effort arises; from the conjunction of ātman and fingers, which depends on that effort, action arises in the fingers; from that, disjunction of bowstring and fingers; from that disjunction, the destruction of conjunction. When that is destroyed, in the absence of an obstruction, when the elastic <s>saṃskāra</s> (dispositional force) present in the bow restores the curved bow to its original position, then from the conjunction of bow and bowstring, which depends on that same <s>saṃskāra</s>, action arises in the bowstring and in the arrow. That [action], without depending on a [further] cause, produces a <s>saṃskāra</s> in the bowstring; the conjunction of arrow and bowstring, depending on that [saṃskāra], constitutes the impulsion (<s>nodana</s>); from that, the first action in the arrow, depending on the impulsion, initiates a <s>saṃskāra</s> in the arrow.

From that <s>saṃskāra</s>, aided by the impulsion, actions continue so long as there is no disjunction of arrow and bowstring. After the disjunction, when the impulsion has ceased, the successive actions [of the arrow arise] from the <s>saṃskāra</s> of the arrow alone, until it falls. Why are there many actions in succession? Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions. But the <s>saṃskāra</s> is single, because in the interval between actions there is no depending-cause [for producing another saṃskāra].
Thus, in bodies presided over by the <s>ātman</s>, action has been stated [to arise] with a cause [involving effort] and without such a cause.

In the four external great elements that are not presided over [by the ātman], action without such a [voluntary] cause — namely, motion — arises from impulsion (<s>nodana</s>) and the like. Therein, impulsion is the specific conjunction that, depending on heaviness, fluidity, impetus, and effort collectively, is the cause of a single action that does not produce disjunction. From that, action arises in all four great elements.

As in earth known as mud. The specific conjunction that, depending on impetus, is the cause of a single action that does not produce disjunction is <s>abhighāta</s> (impact). From that too, action arises in all four great elements — as when hard objects like stones and the like fall upon [something], and likewise when earth known as mud is pushed by feet and the like or is struck. The conjunction that depends on either impulsion or impact, or on both, is <s>saṃyuktasamyoga</s> (conjoined-conjunction). From that too, action arises in earth and the like. And even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck, action arises. For earth and water, in the absence of the conjunction that supports heaviness, and in the absence of effort and impetus, the downward motion due to heaviness — that is <s>patana</s> (falling). As stated in the case of pestles, bodies, and the like. Of these, the first [action arises] from heaviness; the second and subsequent [actions arise] from both heaviness and <s>saṃskāra</s>.

The flowing toward low ground from high ground of water that has become a stream — that is <s>syandana</s> (flowing), due to fluidity. How? The fluidity of the whole, being everywhere obstructed by the conjunctions of the embankment, is checked; the fluidity of the parts, being co-inherent with a single object, is also checked by that same [obstruction]; the successive fluidities of the parts are checked by conjoined-conjunctions. But when a breach in the embankment is made to some degree, then since the fluidity of the whole is everywhere obstructed, there is no origination of its effect; but the fluidity of the part near the breach, since there is no obstruction for the successive fluidities of the parts, obtains its function. From that, the flowing of conjoined [parts] in succession. Then, upon the destruction of the prior substance, by the parts arranged in a continuous series, a long substance is produced, and in that, fluidity is produced through the sequence of causal qualities. And when the causes that are conjoined flow in a continuous series, the action that arises in the whole is called <s>syandana</s> (flowing).

Action from <s>saṃskāra</s> has been stated in the case of arrows and the like. Likewise, in wheels and the like, when conjunction and disjunction arise at the sides of the parts in specific directions and places, the action of the whole that arises from <s>saṃskāra</s> — causing conjunction and disjunction in non-specific directions and places — that is <s>bhramaṇa</s> (rotation). Thus and other specific forms of motion [are explained].

In the wind called <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), action [arises] from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and wind, depending on effort preceded by desire and aversion — in the waking state, this is seen from the fact that [breathing] follows desire; but in the sleeping state, [it arises] depending on effort preceded by vital force. For space, time, direction, and the <s>ātman</s>, even though they have the nature of substances, there is absence of action, because they are incorporeal, like universals and the like. Corporeal form is the dimension of substances that are not all-pervading, and action conforms to it; and that [corporeal form] does not exist in space and the like. Therefore, there is no connection with action for them.

In the mind that is embodied, action [arises] for the purpose of connecting with the other sense organs: in the waking state, from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, depending on effort preceded by desire and aversion — this is established because we observe the successive apprehension of different objects through different sense organs according to intention. In sleep, at the time of awakening, [action arises] depending on effort preceded by vital force. The action of departure and the action of approach [of the mind] arise from the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, depending on <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit). How? When, through enjoyment, the exhaustion or mutual suppression of the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> that cooperate with vital force occurs, then from the deficiency of those cooperating with vital force, and from the consequent deficiency of the effort preceded by them, when the cessation of vital breath occurs, then from other <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> that have obtained their function, aided by the conjunction of <s>ātman</s> and mind, the action of departure — the cause of disjunction from the dead body — arises.

Then, having departed from the body, [the mind] is connected with a transmigrating body (<s>ātivāhikaśarīra</s>) produced by those very <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. And having transmigrated, [the ātman] goes to heaven or hell, and is connected with a body conforming to [its] dispositions. The action for the purpose of that conjunction is the [action of] approach. And for <s>yogins</s>, the going of the externally projected mind to a desired place, and its return. Likewise, at the time of creation, the action for the purpose of connecting with a fresh body is caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>. Thus, whatever else in the great elements that has a cause unapprehended by perception and inference, and that is capable of benefit or harm — that too is caused by <s>adṛṣṭa</s>. Such as: the action of atoms at the beginning of creation; the upward and lateral motion of fire and wind; the hurling of the great elements; the movement of magnetized gems toward a thief; and the attraction of iron toward a lodestone.
Thus [ends] the category of action (<s>karmapadārtha</s>) in the commentary of <s>Praśastapāda</s>.
Now the examination of the category of universal (<s>sāmānyapadārtha</s>).

The universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is of two kinds: supreme (<s>para</s>) and non-supreme (<s>apara</s>). It pervades all instances of its own domain; it is of undifferentiated nature; it resides in many [instances]; in one, two, or many [substances], it produces the cognition of the identity of its own nature; existing continuously in its substrata without difference in its own nature, it is the cause of the cognition of recurrence. How? In each individual [instance], depending on the universal, when cognition arises in a continuous series, and from the <s>saṃskāra</s> produced by the cognition of repeated practice, [and] from the review of the continuous series of past cognitions — that which is recurrent, that is the universal. Therein, the universal of existence (<s>sattā</s>) is the supreme [universal], which is solely the cause of the cognition of recurrence. Just as, in mutually distinct things such as leather, cloth, blankets, and the like, from the connection with the single substance 'blue,' there is the recurrence of the cognition 'blue, blue' — so too, in mutually distinct substance, quality, and action, the undifferentiated recurrence of the cognition 'existent, existent' — and this must come from something other [than the individuals themselves]; that other thing is established as <s>sattā</s> (existence).

Due to the connection with <s>sattā</s> (existence/being), the recurrence of the cognition 'existent, existent' occurs; therefore it is indeed a <s>sāmānya</s> (universal).
The other — <s>dravyatva</s> (substance-ness), <s>guṇatva</s> (quality-ness), <s>karmatva</s> (action-ness), and the like — is both <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) and <s>viśeṣa</s> (particular), since it is the cause of both recurrence and differentiation.
Of these, <s>dravyatva</s> is a universal because it is the cause of recurrence in the mutually distinct earth and so forth, and a particular because it is the cause of differentiation from qualities and actions.
Likewise, <s>guṇatva</s> is a universal because it is the cause of recurrence in the mutually distinct color and so forth, and a particular because it is the cause of differentiation from substances and actions.
Likewise, <s>karmatva</s> is a universal because it is the cause of the recurrence of cognition in the mutually distinct upward motion and so forth, and a particular because it is the cause of differentiation from substances and qualities. Thus, for <s>pṛthivītva</s> (earth-ness), <s>rūpatva</s> (color-ness), <s>utkṣepaṇatva</s> (upward-motion-ness), <s>gotva</s> (cow-ness), <s>ghaṭatva</s> (pot-ness), <s>paṭatva</s> (cloth-ness), and the like — whether pertaining to animate or inanimate things — the status of being both universal and particular is established because they are causes of both recurrence and differentiation.
But these <s>dravyatva</s> and the like, due to having extensive scope, are universals in the primary sense, and due to being differentiators of their own substrata, are called particulars only in a secondary sense.

Due to the difference in definition, the otherness of these from substance, quality, and action as a separate category is established.
And for this very reason, they are eternal.
Due to the restriction of their occurrence in substances and the like, and due to the difference in cognition, their mutual otherness is known.
Each one, in its own substrata, is one, due to the absence of difference in definition and due to the absence of a distinguishing characteristic.
Although universals are not delimited in space, nevertheless, due to the restriction of the instrument of perception and due to the restriction of the aggregate of causes, they pervade all their own objects.
And in the interval, since there is no occurrence through conjunction or <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), they are not designatable.
Thus, in the <s>Praśastapāda Bhāṣya</s>, the category of <s>sāmānya</s> (universal) is completed.
Now, the examination of the category of <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity).

Those that exist in the ultimate entities are ultimate; they are called <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities) because they differentiate their own substrata.
Existing one by one in each eternal substance — the atoms, space, time, direction, <s>ātman</s> (self), and mind — which are devoid of destruction and origination, they are the causes of the cognition of absolute differentiation.
Just as, for people like us, in cows and the like, differentiation in cognition from horses and the like — which have similar shape, qualities, action, and conjunction of parts — is observed: 'This is a cow; it is white; it is fast-moving; it has a large hump; it has a big bell' —
likewise, for <s>yogins</s> (practitioners of yoga) who are more accomplished than us, in atoms that are eternal and similar in shape, qualities, and actions, and in liberated <s>ātmans</s> and minds, since no other cause is possible, those causes from which the differentiation in cognition 'this one is different, this one is different' occurs for each substrate, and recognition 'this is the very same one' occurs even at great distance of space and time regarding an atom — those are the ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities).

But if, without the ultimate <s>viśeṣa</s>, <s>yogins</s> could have differentiation in cognition and recognition from the <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>, then what would happen? It does not happen thus.
Just as a cognition of whiteness does not arise from a <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s> in something that is not white, and recognition does not arise regarding something absolutely never seen before —
if it did, it would be false. Likewise here too, without the ultimate <s>viśeṣa</s>, it is not possible for <s>yogins</s> to have differentiation in cognition or recognition from a <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>.
If one asks: 'Why is differentiation in cognition not postulated as arising from the atoms themselves, just as in the ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s>?' — no, because of identity.
Here, in things that are not self-luminous, cognition arises from another cause — just as in pots and the like, from a lamp; but not in the case of a lamp, from another lamp.
Just as impurity belongs to the flesh of cows, horses, and the like by nature, and to other things through contact with them — so too here, because of identity, differentiation in cognition belongs to the ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s> by nature, and to atoms and the like through contact with them.
Thus, in the <s>Praśastapāda Bhāṣya</s>, the category of <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity) is completed.
Now, the examination of the category of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence).

<s>Samavāya</s> (inherence) is that relation among things that are inseparably connected (<s>ayutasiddha</s>), standing as support and supported, which is the cause of the cognition 'here' or 'in this.'
Among substance, quality, action, universal, and particularity — whether they are in a cause-effect relationship or not — the relation among those that are inseparably connected, standing as support and supported, from which the cognition 'this is here' arises, and from which things that are not omnipresent, whose mutual otherness is known, are not found everywhere — that relation is called <s>samavāya</s>.
How? Just as the cognition 'here in the pot is yogurt' is observed when there is a relation, so too: 'here in the threads is the cloth,' 'here in the reeds is the mat,' 'here in the substance are quality and action,' 'here in substance, quality, and action is <s>sattā</s> (existence),' 'here in substance is <s>dravyatva</s> (substance-ness),' 'here in quality is <s>guṇatva</s> (quality-ness),' 'here in action is <s>karmatva</s> (action-ness),' 'here in eternal substance are the ultimate <s>viśeṣas</s>' — from the observation of such cognitions, it is known that there is a relation among these.

And that is not <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), because the related things are inseparably connected (<s>ayutasiddha</s>), because the occurrence of the cause such as the action of one of them is impossible, because it is not observed to end in disjunction, and because it exists only between the container and the contained.

And it is a separate category from substance and the like, like <s>bhāva</s> (existence), because of the difference in definition.
Just as <s>bhāva</s> — <s>dravyatva</s> and the like — is a separate entity from its own substrata and from each other, because of producing cognitions conforming to itself in its own substrata, so too <s>samavāya</s>, because of the observation of the cognition 'here' in the five categories, is a separate category from them.
And it is not manifold like <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction); like <s>bhāva</s> (existence), it is one everywhere, because of the absence of any distinguishing logical mark, and because of the absence of a distinguishing characteristic. Therefore, like <s>bhāva</s>, <s>samavāya</s> is one everywhere.

But if <s>samavāya</s> is one, then because the relation of substance, quality, and action with their differentiators such as <s>dravyatva</s>, <s>guṇatva</s>, and <s>karmatva</s> would be the same, there would be the undesirable consequence of the confusion of categories. No — due to the restriction of support and supported.
Although <s>samavāya</s> is one and independent everywhere, nevertheless there is a restriction of support and supported.
How? <s>Dravyatva</s> exists only in substances, <s>guṇatva</s> only in qualities, <s>karmatva</s> only in actions.
And so forth. Why? Because of the observation of co-presence and co-absence.
From the observation of the co-presence of the cognition caused by <s>samavāya</s> — 'in this' — it is understood that <s>samavāya</s> is one everywhere.
From the observation of the co-absence of the causes such as <s>dravyatva</s> and the like, the restriction is known.
Just as when the conjunction of pot and yogurt is one, there is a restriction of the support-supported relationship — so too, even when the <s>samavāya</s> of <s>dravyatva</s> and the like is one, due to the difference in the capacity of the manifested and the manifester, there is a restriction of the support-supported relationship.

Even though inherence is a relation, it is not non-eternal like conjunction, because it has no cause, like <s>bhāva</s> (existence).
Just as it was said that <s>bhāva</s> is eternal because no cause is found through valid means of knowledge — so too is <s>samavāya</s>.
For no cause of it is found through valid means of knowledge.
But by what mode of occurrence does <s>samavāya</s> exist in substances and the like?
Conjunction is not possible, since that, being a quality, depends on substance.
Nor is another <s>samavāya</s> possible, since <s>samavāya</s> is one. And there is no other mode of occurrence.
No — because of identity.
Just as for <s>bhāva</s> (existence), whose nature is identical with substance, quality, and action, there is no other connection with <s>sattā</s> (existence) —
so too for <s>samavāya</s>, which is indivisible and whose nature is the mode of occurrence itself, there is no other mode of occurrence. Therefore, it exists through its own nature.

For this very reason it is beyond the senses — like <s>sattā</s> and the like — because there is no occurrence through perceptible things, and because there is no self-perception of itself.
Therefore, <s>samavāya</s> is to be inferred from the cognition 'here.'
Thus, in the <s>Praśastapāda Bhāṣya</s>, the category of <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) is completed.
Homage to <s>Kaṇabhuj</s> (<s>Kaṇāda</s>), who, having pleased <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) through the power of his yogic practice, composed the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> treatise.
Thus is completed the commentary on the six categories beginning with substance, composed by <s>Praśastapāda</s>.
